questions.exp: Section 195 allows an immediate deduction of up to $5,000 (reduced only when costs exceed $50,000), with the remaining $15,000 amortized over 180 months: $15,000 ÷ 180 × 12 = $1,000, for a total of $6,000. Answering $1,333 amortizes all $20,000 and omits the $5,000 immediate deduction.

questions.q: Ray and Sue will acquire rental real estate financed largely with nonrecourse debt and expect large tax losses in the early years. They want to deduct those losses. Which entity choice best supports this goal?
choices: A C corporation, because losses flow through to shareholders
An S corporation, because losses are not subject to basis limits
An S corporation, because shareholders get basis for entity-level debt
An LLC taxed as a partnership, because members include their share of entity liabilities, including qualified nonrecourse financing, in basis and at-risk amounts
questions.exp: Under §752 and §465, partners include their share of partnership debt (including qualified nonrecourse real estate financing) in basis and at-risk amounts, allowing larger loss deductions. S corporation shareholders get basis only for debt the corporation owes directly to them, and C corporation losses do not flow through.

questions.q: Tern Inc. converted from a C corporation to an S corporation two years ago, when it had a net unrealized built-in gain of $300,000. This year it sells land that had a $120,000 built-in gain at conversion, for a recognized gain of $150,000. Taxable income is not a limiting factor. What is Tern's built-in gains tax, assuming a 21% rate?
questions.exp: Under §1374, the recognized built-in gain is limited to the gain that existed at conversion ($120,000), and the tax is $120,000 × 21% = $25,200, well within the NUBIG limit. The $30,000 of post-conversion appreciation is not subject to the tax, so taxing the full $150,000 ($31,500) is wrong.

questions.q: Una is founding a technology startup that she expects to sell in six to eight years for a large gain. She wants to maximize her after-tax proceeds from the sale. Which entity choice gives her access to the §1202 exclusion?
choices: An S corporation
A C corporation, with stock issued to her at formation
An LLC taxed as a partnership
A sole proprietorship that later incorporates by selling its assets to a corporation
questions.exp: Section 1202 applies only to qualified small business stock issued by a C corporation at original issuance, so the gain on a sale after the required holding period can be largely or fully excluded. S corporation stock and partnership interests never qualify.

questions.q: Vale P.C. is a personal service corporation (a qualified PSC) owned by physicians, with average annual gross receipts well above the threshold that normally requires a C corporation to use the accrual method. Which statement is correct?
choices: Vale must use a fiscal year ending September 30
Vale is taxed at a flat 35% rate because it is a personal service corporation
Vale must use the accrual method because its receipts exceed the threshold
Vale may use the cash method because qualified personal service corporations are exempt from the accrual requirement
questions.exp: Section 448 bars C corporations above the gross receipts test from using the cash method but exempts qualified PSCs. Since 2018, PSCs are taxed at the same flat 21% as other C corporations, and they generally use a calendar year unless a business purpose or §444 election applies.

questions.q: Wes contributes land (basis $40,000; FMV $100,000) and Xia contributes $100,000 of cash to form an equal partnership. Two years later, the partnership sells the land for $120,000. How much of the partnership's $80,000 tax gain is allocated to Wes?
questions.exp: Under §704, the $60,000 built-in gain at contribution is allocated entirely to Wes, the contributing partner, and the $20,000 of post-contribution appreciation is shared equally: $60,000 + $10,000 = $70,000. Splitting the whole $80,000 equally ($40,000) ignores the built-in gain rule.

questions.q: Yan contributes a concentrated position in one publicly traded stock to a newly formed partnership, and other investors contribute different publicly traded stocks, producing diversification for each of them. The partnership would be an investment company if incorporated. What is the result?
choices: Yan recognizes gain on the appreciated stock because the transfer to an investment partnership results in diversification
Yan recognizes gain only if he receives cash
The partnership recognizes the gain
No gain is recognized under §721
questions.exp: Section 721 (and §351 for corporations) does not apply to transfers to an investment company that result in diversification of the transferors' interests, so the built-in gain is recognized. This rule blocks exchange funds from diversifying appreciated positions tax-free.

questions.q: Zed owns 60% of Acorn Corp., whose stock is worth $1,000,000 in total. A new investor will contribute cash for a 30% interest. To bring Zed within the control group under §351 as an accommodation transferor under Rev. Proc. 77-37, what is the minimum value of property Zed should contribute in exchange for additional stock?
questions.exp: Under Rev. Proc. 77-37, property transferred by an existing shareholder is not 'of relatively small value' if it is at least 10% of the FMV of the stock he already owns: 10% × $600,000 = $60,000. Using 10% of the corporation's total value ($100,000) misapplies the guideline.

questions.q: Bo transfers equipment held for three years (a §1231 asset) and Cy transfers inventory to a new corporation in a valid §351 exchange. Both receive only stock. Which statement about the holding periods of their stock is correct?
choices: Bo begins a new holding period, while Cy tacks
Bo tacks the equipment's holding period, while Cy's holding period begins on the transfer date
Both begin new holding periods on the transfer date
Both tack the holding periods of the property transferred
questions.exp: Under §1223, stock received for capital assets or §1231 property takes a tacked holding period, but stock received for ordinary-income property such as inventory does not. The corporation's holding period in the property tacks in both cases.

questions.q: Dee contributes appreciated land to a partnership. Eighteen months later, the partnership distributes cash to her that is not a normal operating distribution. What is the main risk?
choices: The distribution reduces the partnership's basis in the land
The distribution is always tax-free as long as it does not exceed her basis
The distribution is treated as a guaranteed payment
The contribution and distribution may be treated as a disguised sale of the land, with gain recognized at the time of the contribution
questions.exp: Under §707 and its regulations, a contribution and a related distribution within two years are presumed to be a sale of the property, which requires gain recognition as of the contribution date unless the facts clearly show otherwise. Relying only on §731 basis recovery ignores the disguised-sale rules.

questions.q: An S corporation's shareholders want the founder to receive a larger share of distributions than her ownership percentage while sharing taxable income pro rata. Which is the likely result?
choices: Disproportionate distributions under the governing provisions may create a second class of stock and terminate the S election
The corporation must file as a partnership
The excess distributions are treated as wages
The arrangement is permitted if documented in a shareholder agreement
questions.exp: Under Reg. 1.1361-1, S corporation shares must confer identical rights to distribution and liquidation proceeds; governing provisions that provide disproportionate distributions create a second class of stock and can terminate the election. Flexible allocations like this require a partnership.

questions.q: Fin is launching a business expected to lose $150,000 in each of its first two years. Fin has $400,000 of salary from another job and will materially participate in the new business. Which entity choice lets Fin use the early losses soonest?
choices: A C corporation, because it can pay Fin a deductible salary
Any entity, because all business losses flow through to owners
A C corporation, because its NOLs can be carried back two years
An S corporation or LLC, because losses flow through and can offset Fin's other income, subject to basis, at-risk, passive, and excess business loss limits
questions.exp: A pass-through entity passes losses to the owner, and with material participation (and within basis and other limits) they offset other income now. A C corporation keeps losses as NOLs usable only against its own future income, and post-2020 NOLs generally cannot be carried back.

questions.q: Gil owns 100% of a profitable C corporation and takes $1,000,000 of salary, far above what comparable executives earn, leaving the corporation with almost no taxable income. On audit, what is the likely result?
choices: Gil's excess salary is excluded from his income
The corporation is converted to an S corporation
The full salary remains deductible because Gil worked full time
The excess salary is reclassified as a dividend: not deductible by the corporation but still taxable to Gil
questions.exp: Only reasonable compensation is deductible under §162; unreasonable compensation to a shareholder-employee is treated as a constructive dividend, which is nondeductible to the corporation and taxable to the shareholder. This is the mirror image of the S corporation issue, where the IRS pushes for more salary.

questions.q: Hu, a physician in a specified service trade or business, has taxable income well above the top of the §199A phase-in range. He is choosing between operating as an S corporation and as a partnership. Which statement about the QBI deduction is correct?
choices: Organizing as a C corporation allows a 20% QBI deduction at the corporate level
The partnership allows a full 20% QBI deduction because guaranteed payments qualify
The S corporation allows a QBI deduction on distributions but not wages
Neither entity yields a QBI deduction for Hu because his SSTB income is excluded above the phase-in range
questions.exp: Above the phase-in range, SSTB income is not qualified business income under §199A, whatever the pass-through form. Guaranteed payments and S corporation wages are never QBI, and C corporations are not eligible for the deduction.

questions.q: Ike transfers fully depreciated equipment (original cost $80,000, basis $0, FMV $50,000) to his new corporation solely for stock in a valid §351 exchange. Which statement is correct?
choices: The corporation recognizes $50,000 of income
Ike recognizes $50,000 of §1245 ordinary income
Ike recognizes $50,000 of capital gain
No gain or recapture is recognized now, but the recapture potential carries over to the corporation
questions.exp: Section 1245 recapture is overridden by §351 nonrecognition except to the extent gain is recognized because of boot. The corporation takes a $0 carryover basis, and the $50,000 recapture potential follows the equipment into the corporation.

questions.q: Jo owns 100% of Pine Corp., worth $900,000. Kai, an unrelated investor, will transfer appreciated land worth $300,000 to Pine for 25% of the stock after the transfer. Jo transfers nothing. What is the result to Kai?
choices: Kai recognizes no gain because he receives only stock
Kai recognizes gain because he does not have 80% control after the exchange
Kai recognizes gain only if Pine pays boot
Kai recognizes no gain because Jo's ownership counts toward control
questions.exp: Section 351 control is measured by the stock owned by the transferors of property immediately after the exchange; Jo is not a transferor, so Kai alone holds 25%, well short of 80%. Kai's realized gain is fully recognized. Jo could join the control group as an accommodation transferor by contributing enough property.

questions.q: Lyn transfers two assets to a corporation in a §351 exchange: Asset X (basis $20,000; FMV $60,000) and Asset Y (basis $50,000; FMV $40,000). She receives $80,000 of stock and $20,000 of cash. What is her total recognized gain or loss?
choices: $12,000 gain and $10,000 loss
questions.exp: Boot is allocated among the assets by relative FMV: 60% ($12,000) to X and 40% ($8,000) to Y. X's realized gain of $40,000 is recognized to the extent of its $12,000 of boot, and Y's $10,000 loss is not recognized under §351. Netting the gain and loss across assets ($30,000 net realized) is not allowed.

questions.q: A newly formed partnership has three partners: an individual with a calendar year, an individual with a calendar year, and a corporation with a June 30 fiscal year. Each owns one-third of profits and capital. Which tax year must the partnership generally use?
choices: A calendar year, because partners owning a majority interest use a calendar year
A fiscal year ending September 30 under a §444 election only
Any year it chooses on its first return
June 30, because a corporate partner controls the choice
questions.exp: Under §706, a partnership must use the tax year of partners owning more than 50% of profits and capital; the two individuals together own two-thirds and use a calendar year. A §444 election or business-purpose year is an exception, not the default.

questions.q: Mo contributes property with an FMV of $100,000 and a basis of $30,000 to a new partnership for a 40% interest. Under the §704 regulations, what are Mo's opening book capital account and his tax basis in his partnership interest, assuming no liabilities?
choices: Book capital $100,000; tax basis $100,000
Book capital $30,000; tax basis $30,000
Book capital $40,000; tax basis $30,000
Book capital $100,000; tax basis $30,000
questions.exp: Book capital accounts record contributed property at FMV ($100,000), while outside tax basis is the contributor's basis under §722 ($30,000). The $70,000 difference is the built-in gain tracked under the contributed-property rules. Using the tax basis for the book account misstates the partners' economic deal.

questions.q: Ned and three other investors form a corporation in a valid §351 exchange. Ned transfers property with a $50,000 basis and an $80,000 FMV and also agrees to perform services worth $20,000, receiving stock worth $100,000. What does Ned recognize, and what is his basis in the stock?
choices: $20,000 ordinary income; $100,000 basis
$20,000 ordinary income; $70,000 basis
$0 income; $50,000 basis
questions.exp: Stock received for services is compensation income ($20,000) even within §351, but the property portion is tax-free. Basis = $50,000 property basis + $20,000 included in income = $70,000. Treating all the stock as received for property ignores the services.

questions.q: Pam wants to bring in investors with different economic deals: one gets a preferred return, another gets 50% of profits but only 20% of losses. She also wants pass-through taxation. Which entity best fits?
choices: A C corporation with two classes of stock
An S corporation with voting and nonvoting stock
An LLC taxed as a partnership
An S corporation
questions.exp: Partnerships may make special allocations that have substantial economic effect under §704, allowing preferred returns and different sharing of profits and losses. S corporations must allocate per share, per day, and may have only one class of stock; voting differences do not change economic rights.

questions.q: Quinn contributes land with a basis of $30,000 and an FMV of $90,000, held as an investment for six years, to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest. What are the partnership's basis and holding period in the land?
choices: $30,000 basis; holding period starts on the contribution date
$90,000 basis; holding period starts on the contribution date
$30,000 basis; holding period includes Quinn's six years
$90,000 basis; holding period includes Quinn's six years
questions.exp: Under §723 the partnership takes Quinn's $30,000 carryover basis, and under §1223 its holding period includes Quinn's holding period. A FMV basis would arise only in a taxable transfer.

questions.q: Rex and Sol own an appreciated operating business and expect to split up in 10 years, with each taking some of the business's real estate. They are choosing between a C corporation and an LLC taxed as a partnership. Which statement about a future in-kind distribution of the appreciated real estate is correct?
choices: A C corporation recognizes gain as if it sold the property, while a partnership distribution of property generally triggers no gain to the partnership or partners
A C corporation's liquidating distribution of appreciated property is tax-free to the corporation under §336
A partnership's distribution of appreciated property always triggers gain to the partnership
Both entities may distribute appreciated property without any entity-level or owner-level gain
questions.exp: Under §311 and §336, a corporation recognizes gain on distributing appreciated property, and the shareholders are also taxed, while under §731 a partnership distribution of property generally produces no gain, with the partners taking a carryover basis. That flexibility on exit is a key reason to choose a partnership for appreciating assets.

questions.q: This year Ali has a $50,000 net §1231 gain. In the prior five years he had $30,000 of net §1231 losses, none of which has been recaptured. How is this year's gain characterized?
choices: $20,000 ordinary income and $30,000 long-term capital gain
$50,000 ordinary income
$50,000 long-term capital gain
$30,000 ordinary income and $20,000 long-term capital gain
questions.exp: Under the §1231 five-year lookback, net §1231 gain is ordinary income to the extent of nonrecaptured net §1231 losses from the prior five years ($30,000), and the remaining $20,000 is long-term capital gain. Treating all $50,000 as capital gain ignores the lookback.

questions.q: Bea owns two business assets held for several years: Asset G, with a $100,000 built-in §1231 gain (no depreciation recapture), and Asset L, with a $100,000 built-in §1231 loss. She has no other §1231 transactions in any year and will sell both over the next two years. Which plan gives the most favorable character?
choices: Sell Asset L in Year 1 and Asset G in Year 2
The order makes no difference because the lookback rule equalizes the results
Sell both in the same year
Sell Asset G in Year 1 and Asset L in Year 2
questions.exp: Selling G first produces $100,000 of long-term capital gain in Year 1, and selling L in Year 2 produces a $100,000 ordinary loss; the lookback looks only backward, so the earlier gain is not recaptured. Selling L first would cause Year 2's gain to be recaptured as ordinary income, and selling both together nets to zero.

questions.q: Cal sells business equipment for $120,000. It cost $100,000, and he had claimed $60,000 of depreciation. How is his gain characterized?
choices: $60,000 ordinary income and $20,000 §1231 gain
$80,000 ordinary income
$20,000 ordinary income and $60,000 §1231 gain
questions.exp: The $80,000 gain ($120,000 − $40,000 adjusted basis) is §1245 ordinary income to the extent of depreciation taken ($60,000), and the $20,000 excess over original cost is §1231 gain. Treating the full $80,000 as ordinary would recapture more than the depreciation actually claimed.

questions.q: Dee, an individual, sells a commercial building (excluding land) held for 12 years for $600,000. It cost $500,000, and she claimed $150,000 of straight-line depreciation. She has no other §1231 transactions or lookback losses. How is the gain characterized?
choices: $250,000 ordinary income
$150,000 unrecaptured §1250 gain taxed at up to 25% and $100,000 long-term capital gain
$250,000 long-term capital gain taxed at 25%
$150,000 ordinary income and $100,000 long-term capital gain
questions.exp: Straight-line depreciation on real property creates no §1250 ordinary recapture for an individual, but the $150,000 of depreciation is unrecaptured §1250 gain taxed at a maximum 25% under §1(h), and the remaining $100,000 is taxed at regular long-term capital gain rates. Treating the depreciation as ordinary recapture applies §1245 rules to real property.

questions.q: Elm Corp., a C corporation, sells a commercial building for $600,000. The building cost $500,000, and $150,000 of straight-line depreciation has been claimed. How much of the gain is ordinary income?
questions.exp: Section 291 requires a corporation to treat 20% of the lesser of depreciation taken or the gain on §1250 property as ordinary income: 20% × $150,000 = $30,000; the remaining $220,000 is §1231 gain. Answering $0 applies the individual rule, under which straight-line depreciation creates no ordinary recapture.

questions.q: Fay and Gil, married filing jointly, were the original purchasers of qualifying §1244 stock for $200,000. They sell it this year for $20,000. How is their $180,000 loss treated?
choices: $180,000 capital loss
$180,000 ordinary loss
$50,000 ordinary loss and $130,000 capital loss
$100,000 ordinary loss and $80,000 capital loss
questions.exp: Section 1244 allows an ordinary loss of up to $100,000 a year on a joint return ($50,000 otherwise); the excess is a capital loss, deductible against capital gains plus $3,000 of ordinary income. The $50,000 limit is for single filers.

questions.q: In 2018, Hu bought newly issued stock of a qualifying C corporation for $500,000 and held it until this year, when he sold it for $12,500,000. The stock qualifies for the 100% §1202 exclusion, and for stock acquired at that time the per-issuer limit is the greater of $10,000,000 or 10 times his basis. How much of his gain is taxable?
questions.exp: The $12,000,000 gain is excluded up to the greater of $10,000,000 or 10 × $500,000 basis ($5,000,000), so $10,000,000 is excluded and $2,000,000 is taxable. Using the 10× basis amount ($7,000,000 taxable) ignores the 'greater of' rule.

questions.q: Ivy wants to qualify for the §1202 qualified small business stock exclusion. Which fact would disqualify her stock?
choices: The corporation's gross assets were well below the statutory limit when the stock was issued
She bought the shares from a founding shareholder rather than from the corporation
The corporation is a C corporation that manufactures medical devices
She has held the stock for six years
questions.exp: Section 1202 requires that the taxpayer acquire the stock at original issuance from a C corporation, in exchange for money, property, or services. Stock bought from another shareholder does not qualify, except for certain gift and death transfers. Manufacturing is a qualified trade or business.

questions.q: Jon sold stock with a $50,000 basis to his son for $30,000, its fair market value. Two years later, the son sold the stock to an unrelated buyer for $60,000. How much gain does the son recognize?
questions.exp: Jon's $20,000 loss is disallowed under §267 because his son is a related party, but under §267 the son may use the disallowed loss to reduce his later gain: ($60,000 − $30,000) − $20,000 = $10,000. The son does not take Jon's $50,000 basis, so a gain computed from that basis is wrong.

questions.q: Kai has a $6,000 long-term capital gain this year. A $10,000 personal loan he made to a friend became totally worthless this year. Kai is not in the business of lending. What is his capital loss carryover to next year?
choices: $4,000 long-term
$1,000 long-term
$1,000 short-term
questions.exp: A nonbusiness bad debt is a short-term capital loss under §166. The $10,000 STCL net of the $6,000 LTCG is a $4,000 net short-term loss; $3,000 offsets ordinary income and $1,000 carries over as short-term. Treating the debt as an ordinary loss ignores the nonbusiness bad-debt rule.

questions.q: Lu bought stock on November 15, 2025, for $40,000. In June 2026 the company became bankrupt and the stock became totally worthless. Lu is a calendar-year individual. How is her loss reported?
choices: $3,000 ordinary loss, with no carryover
$40,000 long-term capital loss
$40,000 short-term capital loss
$40,000 ordinary loss
questions.exp: Under §165, a security that becomes worthless during the year is treated as sold on the last day of the tax year (December 31, 2026), which gives a holding period of more than one year and a long-term capital loss. Using the June date for the holding period would make the loss short-term.

questions.q: Mo inherited stock worth $100,000 at his father's death. His father had bought it for $30,000 a year earlier. Mo sold the stock two months after the death for $110,000. What is Mo's gain and its character?
choices: $10,000 long-term capital gain
$10,000 short-term capital gain
$80,000 long-term capital gain
$80,000 short-term capital gain
questions.exp: Inherited property takes a §1014 basis of $100,000 and is automatically treated as held more than one year under §1223, so the $10,000 gain is long-term regardless of the actual holding period. Using the father's $30,000 basis applies the gift rules.

questions.q: Nan's aunt gave her stock that the aunt bought for $50,000 three years ago; it was worth $35,000 on the date of the gift, and no gift tax was paid. Nan sold it four months later for $30,000. What is Nan's loss and its character?
choices: $5,000 short-term capital loss
$20,000 long-term capital loss
$20,000 short-term capital loss
$5,000 long-term capital loss
questions.exp: Because FMV at the gift was below the donor's basis, Nan's basis for loss is the $35,000 FMV, giving a $5,000 loss; when the FMV basis is used, the donor's holding period does not tack, so the four-month holding period makes the loss short-term. Tacking the aunt's holding period is allowed only when the donor's basis is used.

questions.q: Oli, in the 35% ordinary bracket, sells shares of a physically backed gold ETF, structured as a grantor trust, held for three years at a $40,000 gain. Ignoring the net investment income tax, what is his federal tax on the gain?
questions.exp: Gain on collectibles, including interests in a grantor trust holding physical gold, is taxed at a maximum 28% under §1(h): $40,000 × 28% = $11,200. Applying the 20% or 15% rate treats the ETF like ordinary stock.

questions.q: Pia is a professional painter. She sells a painting she created five years ago for $50,000. Her friend Quinn, an investor, sells a painting he bought from another artist six years ago, realizing a $50,000 gain. How is each gain characterized?
choices: Pia: long-term capital gain; Quinn: long-term capital gain
Pia: long-term capital gain taxed at 28%; Quinn: long-term capital gain taxed at 20%
Pia: §1231 gain; Quinn: ordinary income
Pia: ordinary income; Quinn: long-term capital gain taxed at up to 28% as a collectible
questions.exp: Under §1221, artistic works held by the person who created them are excluded from capital assets, so Pia's gain is ordinary. Quinn's painting is a capital asset and a collectible taxed at up to 28%. The special capital-asset election applies only to self-created musical works, not paintings.

questions.q: Ray, an individual inventor who is not a dealer, transfers all substantial rights to a patent he developed to an unrelated manufacturer in exchange for royalties based on units sold over the next 10 years. He reduced the invention to practice eight months ago. How are the payments taxed?
choices: As long-term capital gain under §1235, regardless of the holding period or the contingent form of payment
As short-term capital gain because the patent was held less than one year
As §1231 gain only if the patent was used in a trade or business
As ordinary royalty income
questions.exp: Section 1235 treats the transfer of all substantial rights to a patent by a holder (generally the individual inventor) to an unrelated party as a sale of a capital asset held more than one year, even when payments are contingent on use. Treating it as ordinary royalty income ignores §1235.

questions.q: Sal is selling his sole proprietorship for $1,000,000. The buyer proposes allocating $100,000 to Sal's covenant not to compete, and Sal suggests allocating that amount to goodwill instead. Sal's goodwill is self-created. Sal is in the 37% ordinary bracket and the 20% capital gain bracket. Ignoring the NIIT, how much does Sal save if the $100,000 is allocated to goodwill?
choices: $0, because both are §197 intangibles
questions.exp: Payments for a covenant not to compete are ordinary income to the seller (37%), while gain on self-created goodwill is capital gain (20%): $100,000 × 17% = $17,000. Both are 15-year §197 intangibles to the buyer, which is why the buyer is indifferent, but the seller is not.

questions.q: Tam buys a business for $1,000,000. The assets acquired are cash of $50,000, accounts receivable with an FMV of $100,000, equipment with an FMV of $300,000, and a building with an FMV of $400,000. No other intangibles are identified. Under the §1060 residual method, how much of the price is allocated to goodwill?
questions.exp: Under the residual method, the price is allocated to Class I through VI assets at FMV, and the remainder goes to Class VII goodwill: $1,000,000 − ($50,000 + $100,000 + $300,000 + $400,000) = $150,000. Leaving out the cash ($200,000) is a common error.

questions.q: Una, a speculator, bought regulated futures contracts two months ago and closed them this year at a $50,000 gain. How is the gain characterized?
choices: $50,000 long-term capital gain
$50,000 short-term capital gain
$50,000 ordinary income
$30,000 long-term and $20,000 short-term capital gain
questions.exp: Section 1256 contracts are marked to market, and gain or loss is treated as 60% long-term and 40% short-term regardless of the holding period: $30,000 long-term and $20,000 short-term. Using the two-month actual holding period ignores the §1256 rule.

questions.q: Vic owns appreciated stock with a $100,000 basis and a $500,000 value. In December, he sells short an identical number of shares of the same stock, intending to deliver his long shares in January. What is the tax effect in December?
choices: Gain is deferred until the long shares have been held for one more year
The short sale is a constructive sale, so Vic recognizes $400,000 of gain in December
No gain until he closes the short sale in January
Only a loss would be recognized in December
questions.exp: Under §1259, entering into a short sale of property substantially identical to an appreciated financial position held by the taxpayer is a constructive sale, so gain is recognized as if the position were sold at FMV. 'Short against the box' no longer defers the gain, with a narrow exception for positions closed by January 30 and held unhedged for 60 days afterward.

questions.q: Win Corp., a C corporation, has $200,000 of ordinary taxable income and a $30,000 net capital loss this year. In the three prior years it had net capital gains of $10,000 (three years ago), $0 (two years ago), and $5,000 (last year). What is its capital loss carryforward after the carryback?
questions.exp: Under §1212, a corporation cannot deduct net capital loss against ordinary income but must carry it back three years and forward five as a short-term loss: $10,000 + $5,000 is absorbed by the carryback, leaving $15,000 to carry forward. The $3,000 annual offset against ordinary income ($27,000 carryforward) applies only to individuals.

questions.q: Xia sold two personal-use assets this year: her personal car (basis $40,000) for $25,000 and her vacation home (basis $500,000, never rented) for $420,000. How much of these losses may she deduct?
choices: $80,000 capital loss
$95,000 capital loss, with $3,000 deductible this year
$15,000 capital loss
questions.exp: Losses on the sale of personal-use property are nondeductible under §165, though gains on such property are taxable. Neither the car nor the vacation home was held for investment or business, so treating them as capital losses is wrong.

questions.q: A flood (not in a federally declared disaster area) completely destroys business equipment with an adjusted basis of $20,000 and a pre-flood FMV of $30,000. Insurance pays $5,000. What is the deductible business casualty loss?
choices: $0, because the area was not federally declared
questions.exp: When business property is completely destroyed, the loss is its adjusted basis less insurance: $20,000 − $5,000 = $15,000; the federal-disaster requirement limits only personal casualty losses. Using the $30,000 FMV would allow a deduction for appreciation never taxed.

questions.q: Yan buys a call option on a stock for a $2,000 premium. Zed, the writer, receives the premium. The option expires unexercised four months later. What are the consequences?
choices: Yan has a $2,000 ordinary loss; Zed has $2,000 of ordinary income
Yan has a $2,000 short-term capital loss; Zed has a $2,000 short-term capital gain
Neither party recognizes anything until the stock is sold
Yan has a $2,000 long-term capital loss; Zed has $2,000 of ordinary income
questions.exp: Under §1234, the holder's loss on a lapsed option has the character of the underlying property (capital) and a holding period of four months (short-term). Under the same section, the writer's gain on lapse is always short-term capital gain. Calling the writer's premium ordinary income is a common mistake.

questions.q: On December 20, Ada sold mutual fund shares in her taxable account at a $15,000 loss. On January 5, her IRA bought shares of the same fund. What is the effect on Ada?
choices: The loss is allowed but deferred until the IRA shares are sold
The loss is disallowed, and no basis increase is available because IRA basis cannot be adjusted
The loss is disallowed, and her IRA basis increases by $15,000
The loss is allowed because the IRA is a separate taxpayer
questions.exp: Under Rev. Rul. 2008-5, a purchase of substantially identical securities by the taxpayer's IRA within 30 days triggers the §1091 wash sale rule, and the disallowed loss is not added to the IRA's basis, so it is permanently lost. The usual basis adjustment cannot apply inside an IRA.

questions.q: Bo bought stock on March 10, 2025, and wants any gain to be long-term. What is the earliest date he can sell the stock and have the gain treated as long-term?
choices: March 9, 2026
March 31, 2026
March 11, 2026
March 10, 2026
questions.exp: The holding period begins the day after acquisition, and long-term treatment requires holding the asset for more than one year, so the earliest qualifying sale date is March 11, 2026. A sale on the anniversary date (March 10) is exactly one year and produces short-term gain.

questions.q: Cy's net long-term capital gain consists of $10,000 of 28%-rate collectibles gain, $20,000 of unrecaptured §1250 gain, and $30,000 of other long-term gain taxed at 15%. He also has a $15,000 net short-term capital loss. After netting, how much of his gain is taxed at the 25% rate?
questions.exp: Under §1(h), a net short-term capital loss offsets the highest-rate groups first: the $15,000 eliminates the $10,000 of 28% gain, then reduces the 25% group by $5,000, leaving $15,000 at 25%. Applying the loss to the 15% group first would leave the full $20,000 at 25%.

questions.q: Dan and Eva, married filing jointly, sell their principal residence, which they owned and lived in for 10 years, at a $200,000 gain. A home office within the dwelling unit gave them $12,000 of depreciation deductions over the past five years. Assuming the $500,000 exclusion otherwise applies, how much gain is taxable?
questions.exp: The §121 exclusion does not apply to gain equal to depreciation claimed after May 6, 1997, so $12,000 is taxable as unrecaptured §1250 gain. Because the office is within the dwelling unit, no allocation of gain between business and residential use is required. Excluding all of the gain ignores the depreciation rule.

questions.q: Under a divorce decree, Fred transfers to his ex-wife, Gina, stock with a $100,000 basis and a $300,000 FMV. A year later, Gina sells the stock for $320,000. How much gain do Fred and Gina recognize?
choices: Fred $0; Gina $20,000
Fred $200,000; Gina $0
Fred $0; Gina $220,000
questions.exp: Section 1041 treats a transfer incident to divorce as a gift: Fred recognizes no gain, and Gina takes his $100,000 carryover basis, so her gain is $320,000 − $100,000 = $220,000. Giving Gina an FMV basis treats the transfer as a taxable sale, which §1041 overrides.

questions.q: Hal bought business equipment for $50,000 and should have claimed $20,000 of depreciation, but he claimed none. He now sells it for $45,000. What is Hal's gain, and how is it characterized?
choices: $15,000 ordinary income
$0 gain
questions.exp: Basis is reduced by depreciation 'allowed or allowable' under §1016, so his adjusted basis is $30,000 and his gain is $15,000. Because the gain is less than the $20,000 of allowable depreciation, all of it is §1245 ordinary income. Using the unreduced $50,000 basis produces a loss. Hal can recover the missed depreciation through an accounting method change.

questions.q: Ian has $200,000 of salary and no capital gains or other §1231 transactions this year, and no §1231 losses in prior years. He will sell one of two loss assets this year: investment land held for five years with a $40,000 loss, or a rental duplex (held for five years and not subject to passive loss limits on sale) with a $40,000 loss. Which sale produces the larger deduction this year?
choices: The duplex, because the net §1231 loss is an ordinary loss fully deductible against salary
Either one, because both produce $40,000 ordinary losses
The land, because a long-term capital loss is fully deductible against salary
Neither, because losses on real property are deferred until reinvestment
questions.exp: A net §1231 loss is ordinary, so the full $40,000 duplex loss offsets salary. The land is a capital asset, so its loss is capital and, with no capital gains, only $3,000 is deductible this year under §1211. Treating both losses as ordinary ignores the capital-asset status of investment land.

questions.q: Jo gives her son business equipment that cost $100,000 and on which she claimed $40,000 of depreciation. The son never uses it in a business and sells it a year later for $90,000. How is the son's gain characterized?
choices: $30,000 ordinary income
$0, because the gift eliminated the depreciation recapture
$30,000 long-term capital gain
questions.exp: A gift is not a disposition that triggers §1245 recapture, but the recapture potential carries over to the donee with the carryover basis of $60,000. The son's $30,000 gain is therefore §1245 ordinary income. Assuming the gift wiped out the recapture is the trap.

questions.q: Kim, a cash-method sole proprietor, sells her business, including $80,000 of accounts receivable (basis $0). How is the gain on the receivables characterized?
choices: §1231 gain
Long-term capital gain
Short-term capital gain
Ordinary income
questions.exp: Accounts receivable acquired for services or inventory sales in the ordinary course of business are excluded from capital assets under §1221, so the $80,000 gain is ordinary income. This is the income she would have reported when collecting the receivables.

questions.q: Lyn acquired newly issued qualified small business stock in August 2025 and expects to sell at a $2,000,000 gain. Assume that for stock acquired after July 4, 2025, the §1202 exclusion is 50% after three years, 75% after four years, and 100% after five years, and that the per-issuer cap is not a factor. If she sells after holding the stock for four years and two months, how much gain is taxable?
questions.exp: After four years, 75% of the gain is excluded: $2,000,000 × 25% = $500,000 taxable (at the 28% rate). Waiting until the five-year mark would make the exclusion 100%. Answering $1,500,000 confuses the excluded and taxable portions.

questions.q: Mapleco, a C corporation, has a $50,000 capital loss carryforward expiring at the end of this year and no capital gains so far. It holds appreciated marketable securities with a $50,000 built-in long-term gain. Which action is best?
choices: Hold the securities, because capital gains of a corporation are taxed at a preferential rate
Deduct the carryforward against ordinary income this year
Sell the securities this year to absorb the expiring carryforward
Carry the loss back three years instead
questions.exp: A corporation's capital losses can offset only capital gains and expire after five years, so recognizing the $50,000 gain this year uses a loss that would otherwise be lost. C corporations get no preferential capital gain rate, and the carryback period for this loss has already passed.

questions.q: Ned sells his sole proprietorship for $250,000, allocated as follows: inventory (FMV $80,000; basis $50,000); equipment (FMV $70,000; adjusted basis $40,000; depreciation taken $50,000); and self-created goodwill (FMV $100,000; basis $0). How much of Ned's gain is ordinary income?
questions.exp: The sale is treated as a sale of individual assets: inventory gain of $30,000 is ordinary, and the $30,000 equipment gain is entirely §1245 recapture (less than the $50,000 of depreciation), so ordinary income totals $60,000; the $100,000 of goodwill gain is capital or §1231 gain. Answering $30,000 overlooks the depreciation recapture on the equipment.

questions.q: Ola bought a business five years ago, paying $150,000 for goodwill, and has claimed $50,000 of §197 amortization on it. She now sells the business, and $180,000 of the price is allocated to goodwill. How is the goodwill gain characterized?
choices: $30,000 ordinary income and $50,000 §1231 gain
$80,000 long-term capital gain
$80,000 ordinary income
$50,000 ordinary income and $30,000 §1231 gain
questions.exp: Section 197 intangibles are treated as depreciable property, so amortization taken is recaptured as §1245 ordinary income ($50,000), and the remaining $30,000 of the $80,000 gain is §1231 gain. Self-created goodwill, by contrast, has no amortization to recapture.

questions.q: Pine Corp. owns 100% of the stock of Sub Co., an operating company that has always earned more than 90% of its gross receipts from active business operations. Sub Co.'s stock becomes worthless this year. Pine's basis in the stock is $3,000,000. How is Pine's loss treated?
choices: No loss until Sub Co. is formally dissolved
$3,000 deductible this year, with the rest carried forward
$3,000,000 capital loss, usable only against capital gains
$3,000,000 ordinary loss
questions.exp: Under §165, a domestic corporation's worthless stock in an affiliated subsidiary (80% or more ownership) that meets the gross-receipts test produces an ordinary loss rather than a capital loss. Without that exception, the loss would be capital and usable only against capital gains, which is why the exception matters in planning.

questions.q: Al and Bo, a married couple, give $50,000 of cash to each of their three adult children this year and elect gift splitting. The annual exclusion is $19,000 per donee. Neither spouse made other gifts. What is each spouse's total taxable gifts for the year?
questions.exp: With gift splitting under §2513, each spouse is treated as giving $25,000 to each child; $25,000 − $19,000 = $6,000 × 3 children = $18,000 each. Taking only one $19,000 exclusion per child ($93,000) ignores the second spouse's exclusions.

questions.q: Cy transfers $100,000 to an irrevocable trust that will pay all income to his daughter for 10 years, then distribute the principal to his grandson. The trustee has no discretion, and no beneficiary has withdrawal rights. The annual exclusion is $19,000. Which statement about the annual exclusion is correct?
choices: A single $19,000 exclusion is available for the trust as a whole
Two $19,000 exclusions are available, one for each beneficiary
No exclusion is available because both interests are future interests
An exclusion is available for the daughter's income interest (up to $19,000) but not for the grandson's remainder
questions.exp: A mandatory income interest beginning immediately is a present interest whose actuarially valued portion qualifies for the exclusion (up to $19,000), while the remainder is a future interest under §2503 that qualifies for none. The trust itself is not the donee, and the remainder beneficiary cannot use an exclusion.

questions.q: Grandma Dee pays $60,000 of tuition directly to her grandson's university, gives him $5,000 to buy textbooks, and gives him a $20,000 check. The annual exclusion is $19,000. What is the amount of her taxable gifts to the grandson?
questions.exp: Tuition paid directly to an educational institution is excluded without limit under §2503, but books are not tuition. The $25,000 of cash ($5,000 + $20,000) less the $19,000 annual exclusion leaves a $6,000 taxable gift. Excluding the book money treats it like direct tuition, which it is not.

questions.q: Eve gives her son stock with a basis of $50,000 and a fair market value of $40,000 on the date of the gift. No gift tax is paid. The son later sells the stock for $45,000. What gain or loss does the son recognize?
choices: $5,000 loss
$5,000 gain
questions.exp: Under §1015 dual basis, the basis for gain is the donor's $50,000 basis and the basis for loss is the $40,000 FMV. A $45,000 sale shows neither a gain under the gain basis nor a loss under the loss basis, so no gain or loss is recognized. A $5,000 loss uses the donor's basis for loss, which the rule does not allow.

questions.q: Fred, age 88 and in poor health, owns publicly traded stock worth $2,000,000 with a basis of $100,000, along with $2,000,000 of cash. His estate will be below the estate tax exemption. He wants to make a large gift to his children now. From an income tax standpoint, which approach is best?
choices: Give the low-basis stock now so the children can sell it at their lower rates
Sell the stock, pay the tax, and give the after-tax proceeds
Give the cash now and keep the low-basis stock until death
Give the stock now and have the children make a §1014 election
questions.exp: Property held until death gets a stepped-up basis under §1014, eliminating the $1,900,000 built-in gain. A gift carries over Fred's $100,000 basis under §1015, so the gain would eventually be taxed. There is no election that gives gifted property a step-up.

questions.q: Gail contributes $100,000 to a §529 plan for her granddaughter and elects to treat the gift as made ratably over five years. The annual exclusion is $19,000. She makes no other gifts to the granddaughter during the five years. What is Gail's taxable gift in the year of the contribution?
questions.exp: The §529 five-year election can spread up to five times the annual exclusion ($95,000), using $19,000 of exclusion each year; the $5,000 excess is a taxable gift in the year of contribution. Spreading the full $100,000 ($20,000 a year, leaving $1,000 taxable each year) misapplies the cap on the election.

questions.q: Hugo, a U.S. citizen, gives his wife, who is not a U.S. citizen, $250,000 of cash. Assume the annual exclusion for gifts to a noncitizen spouse is $194,000. What is Hugo's taxable gift?
questions.exp: The unlimited marital deduction under §2523 is not available for gifts to a noncitizen spouse; instead a higher, inflation-adjusted annual exclusion applies: $250,000 − $194,000 = $56,000. Answering $0 assumes the unlimited marital deduction applies.

questions.q: Ian transfers stock worth $5,000,000 to a two-year grantor retained annuity trust, designed so the present value of his retained annuity equals the value transferred, with the remainder passing to his children. Which statement best describes the result?
choices: The annuity payments are deductible by the trust and taxable to Ian
Any appreciation above the §7520 rate passes to the children free of gift tax, but if Ian dies during the term, the trust assets are generally included in his gross estate
Ian makes a $5,000,000 taxable gift that uses his lifetime exclusion
The children take a stepped-up basis in the remainder
questions.exp: In a zeroed-out GRAT the gift of the remainder is valued near zero under §2702, so growth above the hurdle rate passes gift-tax-free; dying during the term brings the assets back into the estate under §2036. The GRAT is a grantor trust, so annuity payments have no income tax effect, and the remaindermen take carryover basis.

questions.q: Jan transfers her residence to a 12-year qualified personal residence trust, with the remainder passing to her children. Which statement about the transfer is correct?
choices: The taxable gift is the full fair market value of the residence
The children take a basis equal to the fair market value at Jan's death
If Jan survives the 12-year term, the residence is excluded from her gross estate, and if she continues to live there she must pay fair rent
Jan may continue living in the home rent-free for life without estate inclusion
questions.exp: A QPRT gift is only the discounted remainder value, and surviving the term removes the home, including its growth, from the estate. Continuing to live there rent-free after the term would be a retained interest causing inclusion under §2036. The children take carryover basis because they received the home by gift.

questions.q: Kip owns all interests in a family limited partnership holding $10,000,000 of marketable securities. He gives his son a 30% limited partnership interest. A qualified appraiser applies a combined 35% discount for lack of control and lack of marketability. The annual exclusion is $19,000. What is the taxable gift?
questions.exp: The pro rata value of $3,000,000 (30% × $10,000,000) is reduced by the 35% discount to $1,950,000, less the $19,000 annual exclusion: $1,931,000. Answering $2,981,000 ignores the valuation discounts that are the main benefit of the FLP technique.

questions.q: Lu died this year with a taxable estate of $13,000,000. She had made $4,000,000 of post-1976 taxable gifts during her life and paid no gift tax. Assume the basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000 and a flat 40% rate applies to amounts above it. What is her federal estate tax?
questions.exp: Under §2001, adjusted taxable gifts are added to the taxable estate: $13,000,000 + $4,000,000 = $17,000,000, which exceeds the $15,000,000 exclusion by $2,000,000; × 40% = $800,000. Answering $0 compares only the taxable estate with the exclusion and ignores lifetime gifts that already used part of it.

questions.q: Max died this year, using $6,000,000 of his $15,000,000 basic exclusion amount. His executor timely filed Form 706 electing portability. Assume his widow's own basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000 and she has made no taxable gifts. What is her applicable exclusion amount?
questions.exp: The deceased spousal unused exclusion is $15,000,000 − $6,000,000 = $9,000,000, which is added to the widow's own basic exclusion under §2010: $24,000,000. Doubling the exclusion to $30,000,000 ignores the amount Max's estate used.

questions.q: Nan gives $500,000 to her granddaughter. The granddaughter's father, Nan's son, died two years before the gift. Which statement about the generation-skipping transfer tax is correct?
choices: GST tax applies only to transfers in trust
The gift is a taxable termination taxed when the granddaughter dies
Under the predeceased parent rule the granddaughter is treated as Nan's child, so the gift is not a skip
The gift is a direct skip subject to GST tax unless Nan allocates GST exemption
questions.exp: Under §2651, when a lineal descendant's parent who is the transferor's descendant is dead at the time of the transfer, the descendant moves up a generation, so the granddaughter is not a skip person. Without that rule it would be a direct skip, but the parent's death changes the result.

questions.q: Each of the following gifts was made this year, and the annual exclusion is $19,000. Which one requires the donor to file a federal gift tax return (Form 709)?
choices: A father gives his daughter $18,000 cash and makes no other gifts to her
A husband gives his wife, a U.S. citizen, $500,000 of stock
A married couple elects gift splitting for a $30,000 gift to their son made from the husband's account
A grandmother pays $45,000 directly to a hospital for her grandson's surgery
questions.exp: The gift-splitting election under §2513 must be made on a gift tax return, even if each spouse's half falls under the annual exclusion. Gifts to a citizen spouse that qualify for the marital deduction, direct medical payments, and gifts within the annual exclusion generally require no return.

questions.q: Ola transfers $2,000,000 to a revocable living trust for her children, keeping the power to amend or revoke it. Which statement is correct?
choices: Ola makes a completed gift only of the trust income
The transfer is an incomplete gift, and the trust assets will be included in Ola's gross estate
The trust assets avoid estate tax but not probate
Ola makes a completed gift of $2,000,000 less annual exclusions
questions.exp: Keeping the power to revoke means Ola has not parted with dominion and control, so there is no completed gift under Reg. 25.2511-2, and §2038 includes the assets in her gross estate. A revocable trust mainly avoids probate, not estate tax, which is the reverse of the last statement.

questions.q: Pam, age 66, owns undeveloped land worth $1,000,000 with a $100,000 basis. She wants lifetime income, a current income tax deduction, and to avoid paying immediate tax on the gain while diversifying. Which technique best meets these goals?
choices: A gift of the land to a grantor retained annuity trust
An outright gift of the land to a public charity
A sale of the land to her children for an installment note
A charitable remainder unitrust that sells the land and pays her a percentage of the trust's value each year
questions.exp: A CRT under §664 is tax-exempt, so it can sell the land without immediate tax on the gain, pay Pam a lifetime stream, and give her a deduction for the present value of the charity's remainder interest. An outright gift provides no income stream, and a GRAT gives no charitable deduction and no shelter from tax on the gain.

questions.q: Ray owns a $100,000 corporate bond. In December he gives his adult daughter the right to the next year's interest coupons, worth $5,000, while keeping the bond. Who is taxed on the $5,000 of interest when it is paid next year?
choices: Neither, because the transfer is a gift excluded from income
The daughter, because she owns the coupons when they are paid
Ray, because the right to income was assigned without the underlying property
Half to each, under the attribution rules
questions.exp: Under the assignment-of-income doctrine (Helvering v. Horst), income from property is taxed to the owner of the property; giving away only the income right does not shift the tax. To shift the income, Ray must transfer the bond itself.

questions.q: Sid lends his son $90,000 interest-free to buy a home. The loan is payable on demand, has no tax-avoidance purpose, and is the only loan between them. The son's net investment income for the year is $800. For income tax purposes, how much interest is imputed to Sid under §7872?
choices: Interest at the applicable federal rate on $90,000
Interest at the applicable federal rate on $80,000
questions.exp: For gift loans totaling $100,000 or less, imputed interest for income tax purposes is limited to the borrower's net investment income, and it is treated as zero if that income is $1,000 or less. With $800 of net investment income, no interest is imputed. Using the full AFR ignores the $100,000 exception.

questions.q: Two years before her death, Tia gave her nephew stock worth $3,000,000 and paid $400,000 of gift tax. At her death the stock was worth $5,000,000. Considering only these items, how much is included in Tia's gross estate?
questions.exp: Under §2035, gift tax paid on gifts made within three years of death is included in the gross estate, but the gifted stock itself is not (the $3,000,000 enters the tax computation as an adjusted taxable gift, not as gross estate). Including the stock confuses the three-year rule for gift tax with the rule for retained interests and life insurance.

questions.q: Uri, age 70, owns a $3,000,000 life insurance policy on his life and wants to keep the proceeds out of his gross estate. Which plan is most effective?
choices: Have an irrevocable life insurance trust apply for and buy a new policy, funded with Crummey gifts, and surrender the old policy
Name his children as beneficiaries while keeping ownership of the policy
Transfer the policy to an irrevocable life insurance trust and hope to live another year
Name his estate as beneficiary and leave the proceeds to charity by will
questions.exp: Transferring an existing policy brings the proceeds back into the estate under §2035 if Uri dies within three years, but a policy bought from the start by an ILIT that Uri never owned avoids both §2042 and §2035. Keeping ownership while naming the children as beneficiaries still causes inclusion under §2042 because Uri holds incidents of ownership.

questions.q: Val transfers $60,000 to an irrevocable trust for her three grandchildren. Each grandchild has a Crummey power to withdraw up to one-third of the contribution ($20,000) within 30 days, with proper notice, and the powers lapse unexercised. The annual exclusion is $19,000. What is Val's taxable gift?
questions.exp: Each Crummey power makes $20,000 a present interest, so each grandchild's share qualifies for a $19,000 exclusion: 3 × ($20,000 − $19,000) = $3,000. Answering $60,000 treats the whole contribution as a future interest because it is held in trust.

questions.q: Walt deeds his home to his daughter but continues to live there rent-free under an understanding with her until his death 10 years later. What is the estate tax consequence?
choices: Only the value of the home at the gift date is included as an adjusted taxable gift
The home is excluded because a completed gift was made 10 years earlier
The date-of-death value of the home is included in Walt's gross estate under §2036 because he kept possession and enjoyment
The home is included only if Walt dies within three years of the deed
questions.exp: Section 2036 includes property transferred during life when the decedent kept possession or enjoyment under an express or implied agreement, and the inclusion is at date-of-death value. The three-year rule of §2035 is a different provision and does not limit §2036.

questions.q: Xan inherits $800,000 from her mother. She wants the funds to pass instead to her own children, the contingent beneficiaries, without making a taxable gift. Which action achieves this?
choices: Assign her inheritance to her children by written agreement within 12 months
Make a qualified disclaimer in writing within nine months of the death, before accepting any benefits, so the property passes to the contingent beneficiaries without her direction
Disclaim after receiving the first income distribution
Accept the inheritance and give it to her children over several years using annual exclusions
questions.exp: A qualified disclaimer under §2518 must be written, made within nine months, made before any benefits are accepted, and the property must pass without the disclaimant's direction; the property is then treated as never having passed to her. Accepting benefits, or directing who gets the property, makes the transfer a gift by Xan.

questions.q: Yoko made $14,500,000 of taxable gifts in earlier years and makes a $1,000,000 taxable gift (after the annual exclusion) this year. Assume her basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000, she has never been married to a decedent with portability, and a flat 40% rate applies above the exclusion. What gift tax does she owe this year?
questions.exp: Gift tax is cumulative: total taxable gifts of $15,500,000 exceed the $15,000,000 exclusion by $500,000, and 40% × $500,000 = $200,000. Taxing the whole $1,000,000 ignores the $500,000 of exclusion still unused.

questions.q: A married couple living in a community property state owned stock as community property with a basis of $200,000. When the husband died, the stock was worth $1,000,000, and it all passed to his wife. What is the wife's basis in the stock after his death?
questions.exp: Under §1014, both halves of community property get a basis equal to FMV at the first spouse's death if at least half is included in the decedent's estate, so the wife's basis is $1,000,000. The $600,000 answer (half stepped up plus half of the original basis) is the rule for spousal joint tenancy in common-law states.

questions.q: Zack's estate consists of a $2,000,000 traditional IRA and $2,000,000 of appreciated stock. He wants to leave $2,000,000 to charity and $2,000,000 to his children. From an income tax standpoint, which plan is best?
choices: Leave half of each asset to charity and half to the children
Leave the stock to charity and the IRA to the children
Have the IRA distributed to the estate before allocating assets
Leave the IRA to charity and the stock to the children
questions.exp: An IRA is income in respect of a decedent under §691 and gets no basis step-up, so the children would pay income tax on distributions, while a tax-exempt charity pays none. The stock gets a §1014 step-up, so the children can sell it with little or no gain.

questions.q: Ann gives $50,000 to a custodial account for her 8-year-old son under her state's Uniform Transfers to Minors Act and names herself as custodian. She dies when her son is 15. Which statement is correct?
choices: Account income has always been taxed to Ann under the grantor trust rules
The gift did not qualify for the annual exclusion because the son cannot reach the funds until majority
The account is included in Ann's gross estate because she was custodian with power over distributions when she died
The account is excluded from Ann's estate because the gift was completed
questions.exp: UTMA gifts are completed present-interest gifts that qualify for the annual exclusion, but a donor who serves as custodian keeps powers that cause inclusion under §2038 if she dies before the child reaches the age of termination. Naming someone else as custodian avoids this.

questions.q: Bud died this year leaving a gross estate of $20,000,000. Debts and administration expenses are $500,000, and his will leaves $3,000,000 to a qualified public charity and the rest to his adult children. Assume the basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000 and he made no lifetime taxable gifts. What is his taxable estate?
questions.exp: Taxable estate = gross estate less §2053 expenses and §2055 charitable deduction: $20,000,000 − $500,000 − $3,000,000 = $16,500,000. The exclusion is applied through the unified credit against the tax, not subtracted in arriving at the taxable estate, so $1,500,000 is a computation-stage error.

questions.q: Grandpa Cal wants to help with his granddaughter's $40,000 medical bills without using any annual exclusion or lifetime exemption. Which approach achieves this?
choices: Give $20,000 to each of the granddaughter's parents
Give the granddaughter $40,000 to pay the bills
Pay the $40,000 directly to the hospital and physicians
Reimburse the granddaughter after she pays the bills
questions.exp: Section 2503 excludes amounts paid directly to a medical care provider for the donee's medical care, without limit. Reimbursing the donee or giving her cash is an ordinary gift that uses the annual exclusion and possibly the lifetime exemption.

questions.q: Dot owns stock with a basis of $200,000 and an FMV of $120,000. She wants to transfer $120,000 of value to her son. Which approach preserves the most total income tax benefit for the family?
choices: Give the stock to the son so he can sell it and deduct the $80,000 loss
Give the stock to the son and have him hold it until it recovers to $200,000 so he keeps a loss basis
Give the stock to the son, whose basis becomes $200,000 for all purposes
Sell the stock, deduct the $80,000 capital loss, and give the son the $120,000 of cash
questions.exp: Under §1015, a donee's basis for loss is limited to FMV at the gift date when FMV is below the donor's basis, so the $80,000 built-in loss disappears on a gift. Dot should realize the loss herself and give cash. The son cannot deduct her loss.

questions.q: Eli transfers a building worth $500,000, with an adjusted basis of $150,000 and subject to a $200,000 mortgage, to his son, who takes the property subject to the mortgage. What gain does Eli recognize?
questions.exp: A part-gift, part-sale to an individual is a sale to the extent of consideration, and under Reg. 1.1001-1 the transferor's entire basis offsets the amount realized: $200,000 − $150,000 = $50,000. The gift is $300,000. Apportioning basis ($140,000 gain) is the rule only for bargain sales to charity under §1011.

questions.q: Fran sells publicly traded stock held for five years to a public charity for $40,000. The stock is worth $100,000, and her basis is $40,000. What gain does Fran recognize on this bargain sale?
questions.exp: Under §1011 the basis is apportioned between the sale and gift portions: $40,000 × ($40,000 ÷ $100,000) = $16,000, so the gain is $40,000 − $16,000 = $24,000, and the $60,000 gift portion is a charitable contribution. Recognizing no gain applies the part-gift rule for individuals, under which the full basis offsets the amount realized.

questions.q: Gus, a married donor, wants to use his large remaining lifetime exemption before a possible future law change, but worries he and his wife may need the funds later. He transfers assets to an irrevocable trust for his wife and descendants, with his wife as a discretionary beneficiary. How should this spousal lifetime access trust be structured to use his exemption?
choices: Make the transfer a completed gift that does not qualify for the marital deduction and allocate Gus's exemption to it, with his wife getting only indirect access
Have the wife contribute half of the assets so the gift is split
Make the transfer qualify for the gift tax marital deduction by electing QTIP treatment
Have Gus keep the power to revoke the trust if the couple divorces
questions.exp: A SLAT works by making a completed, non-marital gift that uses the donor's exemption while giving the family indirect access through the beneficiary spouse. A QTIP election would bring in the marital deduction and leave the exemption unused, and a retained revocation power makes the gift incomplete.

questions.q: Hal sells closely held stock worth $4,000,000, with a basis of $500,000, to an intentionally defective grantor trust for his children in exchange for a $4,000,000 interest-bearing installment note. What are the income tax consequences to Hal?
choices: The trust takes a $4,000,000 cost basis in the stock
Hal recognizes no gain on the sale, and he is taxed on trust income while the trust remains a grantor trust
Interest paid by the trust to Hal is taxable to Hal and deductible by the trust
Hal recognizes $3,500,000 of gain, reported on the installment method
questions.exp: Under Rev. Rul. 85-13, a grantor and a wholly owned grantor trust are the same taxpayer for income tax purposes, so the sale and note interest are ignored and the trust keeps Hal's $500,000 carryover basis. Hal's payment of the trust's income tax is a further tax-free transfer to his children.

questions.q: Ida gives $3,000,000 directly to her grandson, whose parents are living. She allocates her remaining $1,000,000 of GST exemption to the transfer. Ignore the annual exclusion, and assume a flat 40% GST tax rate. What GST tax is due?
questions.exp: The applicable fraction is $1,000,000 ÷ $3,000,000 = 1/3, so the inclusion ratio is 2/3; GST tax = $3,000,000 × 2/3 × 40% = $800,000. Applying 40% to the full $3,000,000 ignores the exemption allocated.

questions.q: Jon gives his daughter 1,000 shares of a listed stock. On the date of the gift, the stock traded at a high of $52 and a low of $48 and closed at $49. The annual exclusion is $19,000. What is the value of the gift before the annual exclusion?
questions.exp: Under Reg. 25.2512-2, listed stock is valued at the mean of the high and low selling prices on the valuation date: ($52 + $48) ÷ 2 × 1,000 = $50,000. The closing price ($49,000) is not the standard, and $31,000 is the taxable gift after the exclusion, not the value of the gift.

questions.q: Kay's executor elects the alternate valuation date. At Kay's death, Asset 1 was worth $2,000,000 and was still held six months later, when it was worth $1,700,000. Asset 2 was worth $1,000,000 at death and was sold three months after death for $900,000; it would have been worth $800,000 six months after death. What is the gross estate?
questions.exp: Under §2032, property held six months is valued at the six-month date ($1,700,000), and property disposed of within six months is valued on the disposition date ($900,000): $2,600,000 total. Using $800,000 for Asset 2 ignores the rule for property sold before the alternate valuation date.

questions.q: Lars gives his daughter an interest in a growth company worth $1,000,000 and uses a $19,000 annual exclusion, making a $981,000 taxable gift. He dies years later, when the interest is worth $3,000,000. Compared with keeping the interest until death, by how much does the gift reduce the amount subject to the unified transfer tax (taxable estate plus adjusted taxable gifts)? Ignore any gift tax paid.
questions.exp: Holding the interest puts $3,000,000 in the estate; making the gift adds only the $981,000 adjusted taxable gift, valued at the date of the gift, to the estate tax base, a $2,019,000 reduction (the $2,000,000 of post-gift appreciation plus the $19,000 exclusion). Answering $2,000,000 forgets that the annual exclusion portion also escapes the base.

questions.q: Ed and Flo file jointly and expect the same deductions each year: state and local taxes of $10,000 (all deductible), home mortgage interest of $14,000, and cash charitable gifts of $10,000. The standard deduction is $32,200 in each of the next two years. If they instead give $20,000 to charity in Year 1 and nothing in Year 2, by how much do their combined Year 1 and Year 2 deductions increase? Ignore any AGI-based floors or limits on charitable deductions.
questions.exp: Without bunching they itemize $34,000 each year ($68,000). With bunching, Year 1 itemized is $44,000 and Year 2 itemized ($24,000) is below the standard deduction, so they take $32,200: $76,200 total, an $8,200 increase. Assuming the full $10,000 shifted gift is a gain ignores that Year 2 still benefits from the standard deduction only to the extent it exceeds $24,000.

questions.q: Gina, in the 24% ordinary bracket and the 15% long-term capital gain bracket, wants to give $50,000 to a public charity. She owns publicly traded stock held for three years with a fair market value of $50,000 and a basis of $10,000. Compared with selling the stock and donating the cash proceeds, how much federal income tax does she save by donating the stock directly? Assume her deduction is not limited by AGI.
questions.exp: Either way the deduction is $50,000 (long-term capital gain property to a public charity is deducted at FMV under §170(e)). Donating the stock avoids the $40,000 gain, saving $40,000 × 15% = $6,000. The $12,000 figure is the value of the deduction itself, which she gets under both approaches.

questions.q: Hal, age 74, must take a $30,000 required minimum distribution from his traditional IRA this year. He directs his IRA trustee to transfer $20,000 directly to a public charity and has the remaining $10,000 paid to himself. The transfer is within the annual qualified charitable distribution limit, and Hal claims the standard deduction. How much of the IRA distributions does Hal include in gross income?
choices: $30,000, with a $20,000 charitable deduction
questions.exp: A qualified charitable distribution under §408 is excluded from gross income and counts toward the RMD, so only the $10,000 paid to Hal is taxable. Including $30,000 and claiming a deduction is wrong: no deduction is allowed for a QCD, and a standard-deduction taxpayer would get no benefit from one anyway.

questions.q: Ivy, age 12, is a dependent with $6,000 of interest and dividend income and no earned income. For the year, the kiddie tax applies to net unearned income above $2,700 (twice the $1,350 dependent standard deduction for unearned income). How much of Ivy's income is taxed at her parents' marginal rate?
questions.exp: Under §1(g), net unearned income is unearned income less $2,700 (the first $1,350 is offset by the standard deduction and the next $1,350 is taxed at the child's rate): $6,000 − $2,700 = $3,300. Subtracting only $1,350 ($4,650) overlooks the second tier taxed at the child's own rate.

questions.q: Jack's prior-year AGI was $200,000 and his prior-year tax liability was $40,000. He expects current-year tax of $60,000. What is the minimum combined withholding and timely estimated tax payments that will avoid an underpayment penalty under the safe harbors?
questions.exp: Under §6654, the required annual payment is the lesser of 90% of current-year tax ($54,000) or 100% of prior-year tax, raised to 110% when prior-year AGI exceeds $150,000 ($44,000). Using 100% of prior-year tax ($40,000) ignores the 110% rule for higher-income taxpayers.

questions.q: Kara, a single filer, has modified AGI of $260,000, which includes $80,000 of net investment income. The net investment income tax threshold for single filers is $200,000. What is her net investment income tax?
questions.exp: Under §1411 the 3.8% tax applies to the lesser of NII ($80,000) or MAGI over the threshold ($60,000): $60,000 × 3.8% = $2,280. Applying 3.8% to all $80,000 of NII ignores the lesser-of rule.

questions.q: On December 15, Leo sold 100 shares of Zeta stock for $10,000; his basis was $14,000. On January 5, he bought 100 shares of Zeta stock for $11,000. What is Leo's basis in the shares bought on January 5?
questions.exp: The repurchase within 30 days makes the $4,000 loss a disallowed wash sale under §1091; the disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement shares: $11,000 + $4,000 = $15,000. Using the $11,000 cost ignores the basis adjustment that preserves the deferred loss.

questions.q: Mia has realized $25,000 of short-term capital gain this year and no other capital transactions. In December she sells stock held for four years, realizing a $40,000 long-term capital loss. What is her capital loss carryover to next year?
choices: $37,000 long-term
$15,000 long-term
$12,000 short-term
$12,000 long-term
questions.exp: Netting the $25,000 STCG against the $40,000 LTCL yields a $15,000 net long-term capital loss; $3,000 offsets ordinary income under §1211 and $12,000 carries over, retaining its long-term character under §1212. The short-term label is wrong because the excess loss came from the long-term side.

questions.q: Nate, single, bought his home 12 months ago and sold it this year at a $300,000 gain because his employer transferred him to a job 400 miles away. He has never excluded gain on another home sale. How much of the gain is taxable?
questions.exp: A change in place of employment allows a reduced §121 exclusion: $250,000 × 12/24 months = $125,000, so $300,000 − $125,000 = $175,000 is taxable. Applying the full $250,000 exclusion ($50,000 taxable) ignores the two-year ownership and use requirement.

questions.q: Which taxpayer is the strongest candidate for converting a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA this year?
choices: A 63-year-old recent retiree in a temporarily low bracket before Social Security and RMDs begin, who will pay the tax from taxable savings
A 50-year-old who will pay the conversion tax by withholding it from the converted IRA funds
A 58-year-old who expects to withdraw the converted funds next year to buy a vacation home
A 45-year-old in the top bracket who expects a much lower bracket in retirement
questions.exp: A conversion is taxed at current rates, so it pays off when the current bracket is low relative to future rates and the tax is paid from outside funds, leaving the whole balance to grow tax-free. Converting in a high bracket while expecting a lower one later gives up the arbitrage, and withholding the tax from the IRA before age 59½ shrinks the Roth and can trigger the 10% penalty.

questions.q: Olga is in the 35% federal bracket and pays no state income tax. A municipal bond yields 3.5% tax-exempt. What is the minimum yield a fully taxable corporate bond of equal risk must offer to give her an equal after-tax return?
questions.exp: Tax-equivalent yield = tax-exempt yield ÷ (1 − marginal rate) = 3.5% ÷ 0.65 = 5.38%. Multiplying by 1.35 (4.73%) is a common shortcut error that understates the required taxable yield.

questions.q: Pat exercises incentive stock options to buy 1,000 shares at a $20 strike price when the stock is worth $50 per share. Pat holds the shares at year end. What are the regular tax and AMT consequences of the exercise?
choices: No regular tax income and no AMT adjustment
No regular tax income and a $30,000 AMT adjustment
$30,000 long-term capital gain for regular tax and none for AMT
$30,000 ordinary income for both regular tax and AMT
questions.exp: Under §421 no regular income arises when an ISO is exercised, but §56 treats the $30 × 1,000 = $30,000 spread as an AMT adjustment. Recognizing $30,000 of ordinary income describes a nonqualified option.

questions.q: Quinn exercised incentive stock options for 1,000 shares at $20 per share when the FMV was $50, then sold all the shares six months later for $60 per share. What is the character of Quinn's $40,000 total gain?
choices: $40,000 ordinary income
$30,000 ordinary income and $10,000 long-term capital gain
$30,000 ordinary income and $10,000 short-term capital gain
$40,000 long-term capital gain
questions.exp: Selling within one year of exercise is a disqualifying disposition: the $30,000 spread at exercise is compensation income, and the $10,000 post-exercise appreciation is short-term capital gain because the shares were held only six months. Long-term treatment requires holding the shares more than two years from grant and more than one year from exercise.

questions.q: A startup grants Rae 10,000 restricted shares worth $1 each, paying nothing, subject to a three-year vesting requirement. At vesting the shares will likely be worth $10 each. If Rae makes a timely §83 election, how much ordinary income does she recognize at grant and at vesting?
choices: $10,000 at grant and $0 at vesting
$0 at grant and $0 at vesting
$0 at grant and $100,000 at vesting
$10,000 at grant and $90,000 at vesting
questions.exp: A §83 election taxes the $10,000 value at grant as compensation, and nothing further is recognized at vesting; later appreciation is capital gain on sale. Without the election, the $100,000 value at vesting would be ordinary income.

questions.q: Sam actively participates in managing a rental property that produced a $30,000 loss this year. He has no other passive income, and his modified AGI is $130,000. How much of the rental loss can Sam deduct this year?
questions.exp: The $25,000 active-participation allowance under §469(i) is reduced by 50% of MAGI over $100,000: $25,000 − ($30,000 × 50%) = $10,000; the remaining $20,000 is suspended. Using the full $25,000 ignores the phase-out.

questions.q: Tina, a single filer, paid $35,000 of state income and property taxes.
