Assume that for the year the SALT deduction cap is $40,400, reduced (but not below $10,000) by 30% of modified AGI over $505,000. Tina's modified AGI is $560,000. What is her itemized deduction for state and local taxes?
questions.exp: The cap is reduced by 30% × ($560,000 − $505,000) = $16,500, to $23,900, which is less than the $35,000 paid. Deducting the full $35,000 ignores the income-based phase-down of the cap.

questions.q: Uma owns 100% of an S corporation operating in a state that offers an elective pass-through entity tax (PTET). Uma already pays more state tax than the federal SALT cap allows. What is the main federal benefit of having the S corporation elect to pay the PTET?
choices: Uma can claim the PTET as an itemized deduction in addition to her capped SALT deduction
The PTET converts Uma's flow-through income into qualified dividends
The PTET reduces the corporation's built-in gains tax
The PTET is deducted by the S corporation, reducing the flow-through income Uma reports, and is not subject to the individual SALT cap
questions.exp: Under IRS Notice 2020-75, a state tax imposed on and paid by the entity is deductible in computing non-separately stated income, so it reduces Uma's share of income without touching the §164 cap. It is not an additional itemized deduction for Uma, because the entity pays it.

questions.q: Vic, a single filer below the §199A threshold, has $80,000 of qualified business income from a sole proprietorship. His taxable income before the QBI deduction is $90,000, which includes $15,000 of net capital gain. What is his QBI deduction?
questions.exp: The deduction is the lesser of 20% of QBI ($16,000) or 20% of taxable income less net capital gain: 20% × ($90,000 − $15,000) = $15,000. Stopping at 20% of QBI ignores the taxable income limit.

questions.q: Wes, age 56, has family coverage under a high-deductible health plan for the whole year. The HSA contribution limit for family coverage is $8,750, and the catch-up contribution for those 55 or older is $1,000. His employer contributes $3,000 to his HSA. What is the maximum additional amount Wes can contribute and deduct?
questions.exp: Wes's total limit is $8,750 + $1,000 = $9,750, and employer contributions count toward it under §223, leaving $9,750 − $3,000 = $6,750. Leaving out the catch-up gives $5,750.

questions.q: Xena paid $3,500 of qualified tuition for her dependent son's first year of college from her own funds. Her modified AGI is below the phase-out range. What is the maximum American opportunity tax credit she may claim?
questions.exp: The AOTC under §25A(i) is 100% of the first $2,000 of qualified expenses plus 25% of the next $2,000: $2,000 + ($1,500 × 25%) = $2,375. The $2,500 maximum requires $4,000 of expenses, and $700 is 20% of expenses, the lifetime learning credit rate.

questions.q: Yuri is unmarried and has no children. He pays the entire cost of keeping his widowed mother in an assisted-living facility, and she qualifies as his dependent. Yuri lives alone in his own apartment. What is Yuri's most favorable filing status?
choices: Single
Qualifying surviving spouse
Head of household
Married filing separately
questions.exp: Under §2, an unmarried taxpayer can file as head of household by paying more than half the cost of maintaining a household that is the principal home of a dependent parent; the parent need not live with the taxpayer. Defaulting to single misses this exception for parents.

questions.q: Zoe, a cash-method sole proprietor, is in the 22% bracket this year and expects to be in the 35% bracket next year because of a large contract. Ignoring the time value of money, which year-end strategy minimizes her combined two-year tax?
choices: Accelerate both income and deductions into this year
Accelerate income into this year and defer deductible expenses to next year
Defer both income and deductions to next year
Defer billing into next year and prepay deductible expenses this year
questions.exp: When rates are rising, income should be recognized while rates are low and deductions taken when they are worth more, at the 35% rate. The usual year-end advice to defer income and accelerate deductions backfires when next year's rate is higher.

questions.q: A couple in the 32% bracket plans to give appreciated stock to their 17-year-old daughter, who has no earned income, so she can sell it and pay tax at her lower rates. What is the main flaw in this plan?
choices: Capital gains of a minor are always taxed at 28%
The daughter takes a basis equal to FMV, so the built-in gain disappears
A gift to a minor is not a completed gift for income tax purposes
The daughter is subject to the kiddie tax, so her unearned income above the threshold is taxed at her parents' rates
questions.exp: The kiddie tax under §1(g) applies to children under 18 (and to full-time students under 24 whose earned income does not cover half their support), so most of the gain would be taxed at the parents' rates. A gift recipient takes the donor's carryover basis under §1015, so the built-in gain does not disappear.

questions.q: Under a divorce decree finalized in 2022, Alan pays his former spouse $60,000 of alimony a year. Alan is in the 37% bracket and his former spouse is in the 12% bracket. What is the federal income tax treatment of the payments?
choices: Alan deducts $60,000 and the former spouse includes $60,000
Alan gets no deduction and the former spouse includes $60,000
Alan gets no deduction and the former spouse excludes it
Alan deducts $60,000 and the former spouse excludes it
questions.exp: For divorce instruments executed after 2018, the TCJA repealed the §215 deduction and the §71 inclusion, so alimony is neither deductible nor taxable. Deduct-and-include treatment applies only to pre-2019 instruments not modified to adopt the new rules.

questions.q: Bea has $12,000 of investment interest expense. Her investment income consists of $5,000 of taxable interest and $20,000 of long-term capital gain. She has no investment expenses. What is the minimum amount of long-term capital gain Bea must elect to treat as investment income (giving up the preferential rate on it) to deduct all of her investment interest this year?
questions.exp: Under §163, investment interest is deductible only up to net investment income, which includes net capital gain only if the taxpayer elects to tax it at ordinary rates. Bea needs $12,000 − $5,000 = $7,000 more. Electing the full $20,000 needlessly gives up the preferential rate on $13,000.

questions.q: Cal, whose AGI is $100,000, gives a public charity publicly traded stock held for five years, worth $60,000 with a basis of $45,000. He makes no other gifts. If Cal elects to reduce his deduction to basis, what is his current-year charitable deduction? Ignore the 0.5%-of-AGI floor on itemized charitable deductions.
questions.exp: Without the election, the FMV deduction is capped at 30% of AGI ($30,000), with $30,000 carried forward. The §170 election to deduct basis raises the limit to 50% of AGI ($50,000), so the entire $45,000 basis is deductible now, with no carryforward. Choosing $50,000 confuses the limit with the deduction itself.

questions.q: Dana expects to owe alternative minimum tax for the next several years. She is choosing between two municipal bonds with identical yields and risk: a general obligation bond and a specified private activity bond issued after 2008 (not a refunding bond). Which is correct?
choices: The private activity bond is preferable because its interest is exempt from the net investment income tax while general obligation interest is not
The general obligation bond is preferable because interest on specified private activity bonds is an AMT preference item
Both are equally attractive because muni interest is exempt from both regular tax and AMT
The private activity bond is preferable because its interest is an AMT adjustment that reverses later
questions.exp: Interest on specified private activity bonds is a tax preference under §57 and adds to AMTI, so for an AMT taxpayer it is effectively taxable. General obligation bond interest is exempt for AMT. Both types are exempt from the NIIT, so that is not a difference.

questions.q: Eli buys 1,000 shares of a domestic corporation 20 days before the ex-dividend date and sells them 10 days after the ex-dividend date, receiving a $1,500 dividend in between. Eli is in the 32% bracket. How is the dividend taxed?
choices: As a qualified dividend at 15%, because the corporation is domestic
As a return of capital that reduces basis
As a qualified dividend at 0%, because the shares were held less than one year
As ordinary income, because Eli did not hold the shares more than 60 days during the 121-day period beginning 60 days before the ex-dividend date
questions.exp: Under §1, qualified dividend treatment requires holding the stock more than 60 days during the 121-day window around the ex-dividend date. Eli held it 30 days, so the dividend is taxed at his 32% ordinary rate. Being paid by a domestic corporation is necessary but not enough.

questions.q: Fay, a single filer, has a $400,000 net loss from her sole proprietorship and $500,000 of wages. Assume the excess business loss threshold for single filers is $320,000. How much of the business loss is disallowed this year, and how is it treated?
choices: $0, because her wages exceed the loss
$80,000, permanently disallowed
$400,000, suspended until she has business income
$80,000, carried forward as part of a net operating loss
questions.exp: Under §461(l), business losses can offset nonbusiness income only up to the threshold: $400,000 − $320,000 = $80,000 is an excess business loss, which carries forward as an NOL. The loss is not permanently lost, and wages do not count as business income for this test.

questions.q: Gil, a cash-method taxpayer, made the following charitable transfers to qualified public charities near year end. Which one is deductible in the current year?
choices: A check mailed on January 2 that was dated December 31
A gift charged to his credit card on December 30 that he paid off in January
A written pledge signed December 15 to give $10,000 next year
A $5,000 promissory note given to a charity on December 28 and paid in March
questions.exp: A contribution charged to a credit card is deductible in the year of the charge, because Gil incurred a debt to a third party (Rev. Rul. 78-38). A taxpayer's own promissory note or pledge is not a payment until paid, and a check counts only when delivered or mailed, not by the date written on it.

questions.q: Hana itemizes every year and has an AGI of $100,000 each year. She has $4,000 of unreimbursed medical expenses so far this year and expects $2,000 next year. She can schedule a $6,000 elective procedure (not reimbursed) in either December or January. Medical expenses are deductible above 7.5% of AGI. How much more in total medical deductions over the two years does December scheduling produce than January scheduling?
questions.exp: In December: this year $10,000 − $7,500 = $2,500 and next year $0, for $2,500 total. In January: this year $0 and next year $8,000 − $7,500 = $500. The difference is $2,000. Saying $2,500 ignores that January scheduling also gives a small deduction next year.

questions.q: Ian, a single filer, received $20,000 of Social Security benefits, $30,000 of taxable pension and interest income, and $5,000 of tax-exempt interest. Under §86, the base amount for single filers is $25,000 and the adjusted base amount is $34,000. How much of his Social Security is taxable?
questions.exp: Provisional income = $30,000 + $5,000 + 50% × $20,000 = $45,000. Taxable benefits are the lesser of 85% of benefits ($17,000) or 85% × ($45,000 − $34,000) + the lesser of $4,500 or 50% of benefits = $9,350 + $4,500 = $13,850. Defaulting to the 85% cap ignores the formula.

questions.q: Jo, a sole proprietor, hires her 15-year-old son to do legitimate office work and pays him $10,000, a reasonable wage. Which statement about the federal tax effects is correct?
choices: The wages are subject to the kiddie tax at Jo's rate
The wages are deductible but subject to full FICA because the son is a bona fide employee
The wages are not deductible because payments to a minor child are gifts
The wages are deductible by Jo and exempt from Social Security and Medicare taxes
questions.exp: Reasonable wages for real services are deductible under §162, and §3121 exempts wages paid by a parent's sole proprietorship to a child under 18 from FICA. The kiddie tax applies only to unearned income, and the son's standard deduction can shelter much of the wage.

questions.q: Kim and Lou are married and decide to file separate returns. Kim itemizes deductions. Which consequence of filing separately is correct?
choices: Each spouse may claim the American opportunity credit for different children
Lou must also itemize, so his standard deduction is zero
Lou may still claim the full standard deduction for a single filer
The SALT cap is doubled for each separate filer
questions.exp: Under §63, if one spouse filing separately itemizes, the other spouse's standard deduction is zero. Married-filing-separately filers generally cannot claim education credits, and the SALT cap for a separate filer is half the joint amount, not double.

questions.q: Last year Mo itemized deductions of $30,000, including $6,000 of state income tax, all of which was deductible under the SALT cap. His standard deduction last year would have been $29,200. This year he received a $2,000 state income tax refund. How much of the refund must Mo include in this year's gross income?
questions.exp: Under the §111 tax benefit rule, a recovery is taxable only to the extent the prior deduction reduced tax. Itemizing gave him only $800 more than the standard deduction, so $800 is taxable. Including the full $2,000 ignores that he would have received $29,200 regardless.

questions.q: Nia is self-employed, and most of her income is earned in November and December. She has been paying four equal quarterly estimated tax payments based on her expected annual tax. Which approach can legitimately reduce her required April and June payments without a penalty?
choices: Asking her clients to withhold income tax from her payments
Using the annualized income installment method under §6654
Skipping the first two installments and paying the full amount with the return
Paying the full year's estimate on January 15 of the following year
questions.exp: The annualized income installment method bases each required installment on income actually earned through that period, so low early-year income produces low early installments. Skipping installments and catching up later still triggers penalties for the early quarters.

questions.q: Ora, a senior executive in the 37% bracket, expects to be in the 24% bracket after retirement. Her employer offers an unfunded nonqualified deferred compensation plan. Which statement about the plan is correct?
choices: Her election to defer salary generally must be made before the start of the year in which the services are performed, and she is an unsecured creditor of the employer for the deferred amounts
The employer deducts the deferred amounts when they are credited to her account
Deferred amounts are taxable when credited to her account because she has a vested right to them
Deferred amounts can be rolled over tax-free into an IRA at retirement
questions.exp: Section 409A generally requires deferral elections before the year the services are performed, and an unfunded plan leaves the executive as a general creditor, which is the price of avoiding constructive receipt. Under §404 the employer deducts the compensation only when the employee includes it in income, and NQDC cannot be rolled into an IRA.

questions.q: Pia and Rob file jointly. Assume the 0% long-term capital gain rate applies to taxable income up to $98,900. Their taxable income excluding capital gains will be $60,000. How much long-term capital gain can they realize this year and have it taxed at 0%?
questions.exp: Capital gains are stacked on top of ordinary income, so only the room left in the 0% band ($98,900 − $60,000 = $38,900) is taxed at 0%. Treating the whole $98,900 band as available ignores the stacking order.

topics.topic: International tax basics (GILTI, FDII, foreign tax credit)

questions.q: For its 2025 tax year, Domco, a U.S. C corporation, owns 100% of one CFC with $1,000,000 of tested income, $2,000,000 of qualified business asset investment (QBAI) and no tested interest expense. Under the GILTI rules then in effect (net deemed tangible income return of 10% of QBAI), what is Domco's GILTI inclusion before any §78 gross-up?
questions.exp: GILTI = net CFC tested income minus net deemed tangible income return: $1,000,000 - (10% x $2,000,000) = $800,000. The $400,000 trap applies the 50% §250 deduction, which reduces taxable income but not the inclusion itself.

questions.q: For 2025, Domco has a $900,000 GILTI inclusion, an inclusion percentage of 100%, and $100,000 of foreign income taxes attributable to tested income. Assume a 50% §250 deduction, a 21% rate, deemed-paid credit equal to 80% of the attributable taxes, and no expense allocation (the §904 limitation does not bind). What is Domco's net U.S. tax on the GILTI?
questions.exp: Inclusion plus §78 gross-up = $1,000,000; after the 50% §250 deduction, $500,000 x 21% = $105,000, less an FTC of 80% x $100,000 = $80,000, leaves $25,000. The $14,500 trap omits the §78 gross-up.

questions.q: Assume that for tax years beginning after 2025 the GILTI regime (renamed net CFC tested income, NCTI) has no QBAI reduction, a §250 deduction of 40%, and a deemed-paid credit of 90% of attributable foreign taxes. In 2026, Domco's NCTI is $1,000,000 and attributable foreign taxes are $100,000 (inclusion percentage 100%, limitation not binding, 21% rate). What is Domco's net U.S. tax on the NCTI?

For its 2025 tax year, ExportCo has deduction eligible income of $1,000,000, of which $600,000 is foreign-derived, and QBAI of $2,000,000. Assume FDII = deemed intangible income (DEI minus 10% of QBAI) times the foreign-derived ratio, and a §250 FDII deduction of 37.5%. What is ExportCo's FDII deduction?
questions.exp: Deemed intangible income = $1,000,000 - $200,000 = $800,000; FDII = $800,000 x ($600,000 / $1,000,000) = $480,000; and 37.5% x $480,000 = $180,000. The $225,000 trap applies 37.5% to the $600,000 of foreign-derived DEI without removing the deemed tangible return.

questions.q: Worldco, a U.S. corporation, has worldwide taxable income of $1,000,000, including $400,000 of foreign-source general-category taxable income. Its precredit U.S. tax is $210,000, and it paid $100,000 of foreign income taxes on the general-category income. What foreign tax credit may Worldco claim this year?
questions.exp: The §904 limitation is $210,000 x ($400,000 / $1,000,000) = $84,000, which is less than the $100,000 paid, so the credit is $84,000. The $16,000 excess can be carried back 1 year and forward 10 years.

questions.q: In 2025, a U.S. corporation's foreign income taxes deemed paid on its GILTI exceed its §904 limitation for the GILTI basket by $30,000. What happens to the $30,000?
choices: It may be used against general-category income
It cannot be carried back or forward and is permanently lost
It may be deducted instead of credited in the same year
It is carried back 1 year and forward 10 years
questions.exp: Excess GILTI-basket credits have no carryback or carryforward under §904, so they are lost. The 1-back/10-forward rule applies only to other baskets, and income cannot be moved between baskets.

questions.q: Sam, a single U.S. individual, has only passive foreign-source income, all reported on payee statements, with $250 of creditable foreign taxes withheld. Which statement about Sam's foreign tax credit is correct?
choices: He may only deduct the tax because it is under $300
He may claim the credit only if he itemizes deductions
He may elect to claim the full $250 credit without Form 1116 and without the §904 limitation
He must file Form 1116 to claim any credit
questions.exp: The §904(j) de minimis election lets individuals with only passive income and creditable foreign taxes of $300 or less ($600 if married filing jointly) claim the credit without Form 1116 or the limitation. A credit, unlike a deduction, does not require itemizing.

questions.q: SellCo, a CFC incorporated in Country X, buys products from its U.S. parent and resells them to unrelated customers in Country Y for use there. SellCo has no manufacturing activity. How is SellCo's sales profit classified?
choices: Foreign personal holding company income
Exempt because it is active business income
Tested income for GILTI only, because the customers are unrelated
Foreign base company sales income, a type of Subpart F income
questions.exp: Buying from a related person and selling property made and used outside the CFC's country of incorporation is foreign base company sales income under §954. Unrelated customers do not prevent the classification, because the purchase was from a related party.

questions.q: ForCo, a foreign corporation, is owned by the following unrelated persons (vote and value): Ann (U.S. citizen) 30%, Bix Corp. (U.S.) 25%, Carl (U.S. citizen) 9%, Dee (U.S. citizen) 8%, and a foreign individual 28%. ForCo has Subpart F income. Who must include a share of ForCo's Subpart F income?
choices: No one, because no U.S. person owns more than 50%
Ann, Bix Corp., Carl and Dee
Ann only
Ann and Bix Corp. only
questions.exp: U.S. shareholders (10% or more) Ann and Bix together own 55%, which makes ForCo a CFC, and only U.S. shareholders include Subpart F income. Carl and Dee are under 10%, so they are not U.S. shareholders even though U.S. persons own 72% in total.

questions.q: With a 21% U.S. corporate rate, a CFC may elect to exclude high-taxed income from Subpart F if the foreign effective tax rate exceeds 90% of the U.S. rate. Which foreign effective rate on a CFC's foreign base company income qualifies?
questions.exp: The threshold is 90% x 21% = 18.9%, and only 19% exceeds it. The 18% rate is the trap: it is close to the threshold but below 18.9%.

questions.q: USCo has owned 20% of a foreign corporation for three years. It receives a $500,000 foreign-source dividend (not a hybrid dividend) from undistributed non-PTEP earnings, with $50,000 of foreign withholding tax. What is the U.S. tax treatment?
choices: $500,000 is taxable with a $50,000 foreign tax credit
A 65% dividends-received deduction applies, with a credit for the withholding tax
A $500,000 §245A deduction applies, and the $50,000 withholding is neither creditable nor deductible
$500,000 is taxable with a $50,000 deduction for the withholding tax
questions.exp: §245A gives a 100% DRD for the foreign-source portion of dividends from a specified 10%-owned foreign corporation when the holding period is met, and §245A denies both the credit and the deduction for related foreign taxes. The 65% DRD applies to domestic dividends, not this case.

questions.q: Lia, a U.S. citizen, met the physical presence test for 300 days of 2025 (a 365-day year) and earned $150,000 of foreign wages during that period. Assume the 2025 maximum foreign earned income exclusion is $130,000. What is her foreign earned income exclusion?
questions.exp: The exclusion is prorated by qualifying days: $130,000 x 300 / 365 = $106,849. Claiming the full $130,000 ignores the proration.

questions.q: Assume for 2025 a $130,000 maximum foreign earned income exclusion, a housing base amount of 16% of that maximum ($20,800), and a housing expense cap of 30% of that maximum ($39,000) for Mark's foreign city. Mark qualifies for the full year, paid $40,000 of qualifying housing expenses, and his earned income is well above the exclusions. What is his foreign housing exclusion?
questions.exp: Housing expenses are capped at $39,000, and the exclusion is $39,000 - $20,800 base = $18,200. The $19,200 trap subtracts the base from the uncapped $40,000.

questions.q: A profitable U.S. corporation is entering a new foreign market and expects large operating losses for the first three years. If its goal is to use those losses against U.S. income as they occur, which structure is generally best?
choices: A foreign corporation treated as a corporation for U.S. tax purposes
A foreign branch or a foreign entity treated as disregarded under the check-the-box rules
A CFC whose losses offset Subpart F income of other CFCs
A domestic subsidiary that does not join the consolidated return
questions.exp: Branch or disregarded-entity losses flow directly into the U.S. corporation's return. Losses of a foreign corporation stay inside it (a tested loss only offsets other CFCs' tested income), and a nonconsolidated subsidiary's losses stay with that subsidiary.

questions.q: A newly formed foreign eligible entity has two members, each with limited liability under local law, and makes no entity classification election. What is its default U.S. tax classification?
choices: Trust
Partnership
Association taxable as a corporation
Disregarded entity
questions.exp: Under Reg. §301.7701-3, a foreign eligible entity is a corporation by default if no member has unlimited liability. Partnership treatment is the default only if at least one member has unlimited liability, or under the domestic default rules.

questions.q: USCo transfers appreciated equipment (FMV $900,000, basis $500,000) to its newly formed wholly owned foreign subsidiary in exchange for stock, in a transaction that would qualify under §351 if both corporations were domestic. How much gain does USCo recognize?
choices: $0 now, with gain deferred until the foreign subsidiary sells the equipment
$0, because §351 applies
Gain only to the extent of depreciation recapture
questions.exp: §367 treats the foreign transferee as not being a corporation for nonrecognition purposes, so USCo recognizes the $400,000 gain on the outbound transfer of tangible property. Assuming §351 still applies is the trap.

questions.q: A U.S. parent sells goods to its foreign distribution subsidiary, which resells them to unrelated customers for $1,000,000. Comparable independent distributors earn a 25% gross margin. Under the §482 resale price method, what is the arm's-length price the subsidiary pays the parent?
questions.exp: Resale price minus the appropriate gross profit: $1,000,000 - (25% x $1,000,000) = $750,000. Treating 25% as a markup on cost ($1,000,000 / 1.25 = $800,000) confuses this method with cost plus.

questions.q: USCo pays a $100,000 royalty for use of a patent in the United States to a foreign company resident in a treaty country. The treaty reduces the royalty withholding rate to 10%, and the payee gave USCo a valid Form W-8BEN-E claiming treaty benefits. How much must USCo withhold?
questions.exp: Royalties are FDAP income subject to 30% withholding, reduced to the treaty rate (10% x $100,000 = $10,000) when the payee documents its eligibility. Without valid documentation, USCo would have to withhold $30,000.

questions.q: A nonresident alien individual holds a registered bond issued by an unrelated U.S. corporation and owns no stock in the issuer. She provides a valid Form W-8BEN. What U.S. tax applies to the $40,000 of interest she receives?
choices: Graduated rates as effectively connected income
None, under the portfolio interest exemption
30% withholding, or $12,000
15% FIRPTA withholding
questions.exp: Portfolio interest paid to a documented foreign person who owns less than 10% of the issuer is exempt from U.S. tax under §871(h). FIRPTA applies only to U.S. real property interests.

questions.q: A foreign individual sells a U.S. office building for $2,000,000. His adjusted basis is $1,200,000. Under the general FIRPTA withholding rule (§1445), how much must the buyer withhold?
questions.exp: FIRPTA withholding is generally 15% of the amount realized, not the gain: 15% x $2,000,000 = $300,000. The $120,000 trap applies 15% to the $800,000 gain.

questions.q: ForCorp, a foreign corporation, has $1,000,000 of effectively connected taxable income and pays $210,000 of U.S. income tax. Its U.S. net equity did not change during the year, and no treaty applies. What is ForCorp's branch profits tax?
questions.exp: The dividend equivalent amount is effectively connected E&P of $1,000,000 - $210,000 = $790,000 (no change in net equity), and 30% x $790,000 = $237,000. The $300,000 trap applies 30% before subtracting the U.S. income tax.

questions.q: For 2025, a U.S. corporation owns two CFCs. CFC 1 has tested income of $900,000 and QBAI of $1,000,000. CFC 2 has a tested loss of $300,000 and QBAI of $500,000. With no tested interest expense and a 10% deemed return on QBAI, what is the GILTI inclusion?
questions.exp: Net tested income is $900,000 - $300,000 = $600,000, and only tested-income CFCs' QBAI counts: 10% x $1,000,000 = $100,000, so GILTI = $500,000. The $450,000 trap also counts the QBAI of the tested-loss CFC.

questions.q: A U.S. corporation makes the GILTI high-tax exclusion election for a CFC whose tested income bears a foreign effective rate above 18.9%. What is a consequence of the election?
choices: The CFC's QBAI is doubled in computing the deemed tangible return
The excluded income is taxed as Subpart F income instead
The excluded income is not tested income, and foreign taxes on it are not creditable
The foreign taxes on the excluded income may be carried forward 10 years
questions.exp: High-taxed income excluded from tested income produces no GILTI inclusion, so no deemed-paid credit is available for its foreign taxes. The election can also eliminate QBAI attributable to the excluded income, so it can reduce rather than increase the deemed return.

questions.q: A U.S. distributor buys inventory from U.S. suppliers and sells it to customers in Germany, with title passing in Germany. The distributor does no manufacturing. What is the source of the sales income for foreign tax credit purposes?
choices: U.S. source, because the inventory was purchased in the United States
Foreign source, because title passed outside the United States
U.S. source, because the seller is a U.S. resident
Split 50/50 between U.S. and foreign source
questions.exp: Gain on purchased inventory is sourced where title passes (§861 and §862), so it is foreign source. The 50/50 split was the old rule for inventory the seller produced, not purchased.

questions.q: Jo, a U.S. consultant, received $200,000 for a project requiring 100 workdays, of which 40 days were worked in Canada and 60 in the United States. How much of the fee is foreign-source income?
questions.exp: Compensation for personal services is sourced where the services are performed, so $200,000 x 40 / 100 = $80,000 is foreign source. Sourcing by the payer's residence or the taxpayer's citizenship is the trap.

questions.q: Rhea, a U.S. individual, owns 15% of a CFC. Her CFC earned $300,000 of Subpart F income that she included in prior years. This year the CFC distributes $500,000 to her from its earnings, which total $800,000 including the $300,000 already taxed. How much of the distribution is a taxable dividend?
questions.exp: Distributions come first from previously taxed E&P, which is excluded under §959, so $300,000 is tax-free and the remaining $200,000 is a taxable dividend. As an individual, Rhea cannot claim the §245A deduction.

questions.q: Tom, a U.S. citizen, had three foreign bank accounts during the year, with maximum balances (reached at different times) of $4,000, $3,500 and $3,000. What is his FBAR (FinCEN Form 114) filing obligation?
choices: None, because the balances never exceeded $10,000 on the same day
He must file, because the aggregate of the accounts' maximum values ($10,500) exceeded $10,000
He must file only if the accounts earned more than $10,000 of income
None, because no single account exceeded $10,000
questions.exp: The FBAR threshold is an aggregate maximum value above $10,000 at any time during the year, computed by summing each account's maximum value: $4,000 + $3,500 + $3,000 = $10,500. The test does not look at individual accounts or a single day.

questions.q: Pat, a U.S. citizen living in the U.K., is a U.K. resident under the U.S.-U.K. treaty tie-breaker rules. She argues the treaty exempts her U.K. wages from U.S. tax. What is the correct analysis?
choices: She is exempt only if U.K. tax exceeds U.S. tax
She is correct, because the treaty assigns taxing rights to her residence country
She is correct only if she files Form 8833
Under the treaty's saving clause, the United States may tax its citizens as if the treaty did not exist, although she may claim the FEIE or a foreign tax credit
questions.exp: U.S. treaties contain a saving clause preserving U.S. taxation of citizens, so relief comes from the FEIE or the FTC rather than from treaty exemption. Form 8833 discloses treaty positions but cannot override the saving clause.

questions.q: For 2025, which of the following is foreign-derived deduction eligible income of a U.S. C corporation for FDII purposes?
choices: Profit on a sale of equipment to an unrelated foreign customer for use outside the United States
GILTI inclusions from its CFCs
Profit on a sale to a U.S. wholesaler that later exports the goods
Income earned through its foreign branch
questions.exp: FDDEI includes income from sales of property to foreign persons for foreign use and from services provided to persons located abroad. GILTI, Subpart F, dividends and foreign branch income are excluded from deduction eligible income, and a sale to a U.S. person for resale generally does not qualify.

questions.q: Assume a 10% BEAT rate. A large U.S. corporation that meets the BEAT gross receipts and base erosion percentage thresholds has taxable income of $100 million after deducting $40 million of base erosion payments to foreign affiliates. Its regular tax liability, net of allowable credits, is $9 million. What is its BEAT liability?
choices: $4 million
$14 million
$5 million
questions.exp: Modified taxable income = $100M + $40M = $140M, and 10% x $140M = $14M; BEAT is the excess over the $9M regular tax, or $5M. The $14M trap forgets to subtract the regular tax liability.

questions.q: Assume a 2025 foreign earned income exclusion of $130,000. Nina earned $150,000 of foreign wages, excluded $130,000, and paid $30,000 of foreign income tax on the wages. Before applying the §904 limitation, how much of the foreign tax is eligible for credit?
questions.exp: Foreign taxes allocable to excluded income are not creditable: $30,000 x $130,000 / $150,000 = $26,000 is disallowed, leaving $4,000. Claiming all $30,000 double-dips with the exclusion.

questions.q: Assume a 2025 exclusion amount of $890,000 under §877A. Ron, a covered expatriate, renounces citizenship holding assets with $3,000,000 of unrealized gain (no deferred compensation or trust interests). What net gain does the mark-to-market regime treat as recognized?
questions.exp: Under §877A, property is deemed sold the day before expatriation, and gain is reduced by the inflation-adjusted exclusion: $3,000,000 - $890,000 = $2,110,000. Expatriating does not avoid the exit tax.

questions.q: USCo's wholly owned CFC earned $500,000 of pretax foreign base company income and paid $100,000 of foreign income tax on it. Assuming a 21% rate, no §250 deduction for Subpart F income, and the §904 limitation not binding, what is USCo's net U.S. tax on the Subpart F inclusion?
questions.exp: Inclusion of $400,000 plus §78 gross-up of $100,000 = $500,000 x 21% = $105,000, less a full §960 deemed-paid credit of $100,000 = $5,000. The 80% haircut applies only to GILTI, not Subpart F.

questions.q: A CFC has $30,000,000 of gross income, of which $1,200,000 is foreign base company income. Under the §954 de minimis rule, none of a CFC's gross income is treated as FBCI if FBCI is less than the lesser of 5% of gross income or $1,000,000. How much FBCI does the CFC have?
choices: $0, because FBCI is under 5% of gross income
questions.exp: The de minimis threshold is the lesser of $1,500,000 (5%) or $1,000,000, so $1,000,000; because $1,200,000 exceeds it, all of the FBCI counts, not just the excess. The full-inclusion rule (all gross income) applies only when FBCI exceeds 70% of gross income.

questions.q: Hal, a U.S. individual, owns 100% of a profitable foreign corporation that is a CFC generating large GILTI inclusions taxed at his 37% individual rate. Which planning election could most directly lower the current U.S. tax on the GILTI?
choices: Electing to treat the CFC as a partnership
Making a §962 election to be taxed at corporate rates, with access to the §250 deduction and deemed-paid credits
Electing the foreign earned income exclusion
Electing to deduct rather than credit foreign taxes
questions.exp: A §962 election lets an individual U.S. shareholder be taxed on Subpart F and GILTI as if a domestic corporation, using the 21% rate, the §250 deduction and indirect credits, though later distributions are taxed again. The FEIE covers earned income only, not CFC inclusions.

questions.q: EuroCo, a resident of a treaty country, sells goods to U.S. customers through an independent commission agent acting in the ordinary course of its own business, and has no U.S. office. Under the business profits article of a typical U.S. income tax treaty, how are EuroCo's U.S. sales profits treated?
choices: Taxed at 30% as FDAP income
Not subject to U.S. income tax, because EuroCo has no U.S. permanent establishment
Taxed as effectively connected income at 21%
Subject to the branch profits tax only
questions.exp: Treaties allow the source country to tax business profits only if they are attributable to a permanent establishment, and an independent agent acting in its ordinary course does not create one. Business profits are not FDAP income.

questions.q: USCo's foreign subsidiary pays several foreign levies. Which one is most likely creditable under §901 as a foreign income tax?
choices: A payroll tax for the local social security system on employer wages
A customs duty on imported components
Value-added tax collected on the subsidiary's sales
Corporate income tax on net income, or a withholding tax imposed in lieu of an income tax
questions.exp: Creditable taxes are income taxes, or taxes in lieu of them under §903, such as withholding taxes on dividends or royalties. VAT, payroll and customs levies are not income taxes, though they may be deductible.

questions.q: Why does a domestic corporation claiming a deemed-paid foreign tax credit for Subpart F or GILTI income include a §78 gross-up in income?
choices: To put the corporation in the same position as if it had earned the pretax foreign income directly and paid the foreign tax itself
To convert the foreign tax into a deduction
To recapture foreign losses previously deducted
To penalize income deferred offshore
questions.exp: Without the gross-up, the corporation would be taxed on after-tax income while also crediting the tax, effectively getting both a deduction and a credit. §78 adds the deemed-paid taxes to income so the credit reflects pretax income.

questions.q: Delta Corp. is taxable in State X, which apportions business income using a three-factor formula with a double-weighted sales factor. Delta's State X property is $2,000,000 of $8,000,000 total, State X payroll is $3,000,000 of $6,000,000 total, and State X sales are $4,000,000 of $20,000,000 total. Delta's apportionable business income is $1,000,000. How much business income is apportioned to State X?
questions.exp: Factors are 25% property, 50% payroll and 20% sales; with sales double-weighted, (25% + 50% + 20% + 20%) / 4 = 28.75%, and 28.75% x $1,000,000 = $287,500. The $316,667 trap uses an equally weighted three-factor formula (95% / 3).

questions.q: Glenn Co. sells industrial pumps into State M. Its salespeople solicit orders there, all orders are approved at headquarters in another state, and pumps are shipped from an out-of-state warehouse. This year one State M salesperson also began regularly installing and repairing pumps at customer sites. What is the effect on Glenn's State M net income tax exposure?
choices: Glenn becomes subject only to State M sales tax, not income tax
Glenn loses Public Law 86-272 protection because installation and repair are not ancillary to solicitation, so Glenn is subject to State M net income tax
Glenn is subject to State M income tax only on the repair fees, while pump sales remain protected
None, because orders are still approved and shipped from outside State M
questions.exp: P.L. 86-272 protects only solicitation of orders for tangible personal property and activities ancillary to it; regular installation and repair services exceed that safe harbor, so protection is lost for the whole year's income. Protection is not split by revenue stream, which is the trap in the repair-fees-only choice.

questions.q: After South Dakota v. Wayfair, State R requires remote sellers to collect sales tax if, in the current or prior calendar year, they have more than $100,000 of sales into the state or 200 or more separate transactions. Bloom LLC, with no physical presence in State R, made 250 sales totaling $80,000 to State R customers last year. What is Bloom's State R sales tax obligation?
choices: Bloom must register and collect State R sales tax because it met the transaction threshold
Bloom must collect tax only on sales above the first $100,000
None, because it has no physical presence in State R
None, because its sales did not exceed $100,000
questions.exp: The thresholds are alternative tests, so 250 transactions alone creates economic nexus even though dollar sales were below $100,000. Wayfair eliminated the physical-presence requirement for sales tax collection.

questions.q: Arc Corp. is taxable in State A, which has a throwback rule. Arc ships goods from its State A plant: $3,000,000 to State A customers, $2,000,000 to State B customers (Arc is not taxable in State B because of P.L. 86-272), and $5,000,000 to State C customers (Arc is taxable in State C). What is Arc's State A sales factor?
questions.exp: Under throwback, sales shipped from State A into a state where Arc is not taxable are added back to the State A numerator: ($3,000,000 + $2,000,000) / $10,000,000 = 50%. The 30% trap ignores the throwback of the State B sales.

questions.q: State D uses a single sales factor with a throwout rule. Fin Co. had $4,000,000 of sales to State D customers, $4,000,000 to customers in states where Fin is taxable, and $2,000,000 to customers in states where Fin is not taxable. What is Fin's State D apportionment percentage?
questions.exp: Throwout removes the $2,000,000 of 'nowhere' sales from the denominator: $4,000,000 / $8,000,000 = 50%. The 40% choice ignores the rule, and 60% applies throwback instead of throwout.

questions.q: Pine Consulting performs all of its services with employees located in State A for clients located in State B. State A sources service receipts by cost of performance; State B uses market-based sourcing. Pine is taxable in both states. Which result is most likely for Pine's service receipts?
choices: They are included in neither state's sales factor numerator
They are included only in State A's numerator, because the services are performed there
They are included in the sales factor numerator of both State A and State B
They are included only in State B's numerator, because market sourcing overrides cost of performance
questions.exp: Each state applies its own sourcing rule, so State A sources the receipts where the work is performed and State B sources them to the customer's location, risking more than 100% apportionment. There is no federal rule that makes one state's method override the other's.

questions.q: A unitary group files a combined report in State K, which uses a single sales factor and the Finnigan approach. Parent (taxable in State K) had $2,000,000 of State K sales; Sub (no State K nexus) had $3,000,000 of State K sales. Group sales everywhere were $20,000,000 and combined business income was $4,000,000. How much combined income is apportioned to State K?
questions.exp: Under Finnigan, the numerator includes all group members' State K sales, even those without nexus: ($2,000,000 + $3,000,000) / $20,000,000 = 25%, x $4,000,000 = $1,000,000. The $400,000 trap uses the Joyce approach, counting only the nexus member's sales (10%).

questions.q: Crest Corp. is commercially domiciled in State A and does business in States A and B. This year it received $100,000 of dividends and $50,000 of rents from land in State B, both properly classified as nonbusiness income. Under UDITPA allocation rules, how much nonbusiness income is allocated to State B?
questions.exp: Nonbusiness rents from real property are allocated to the state where the property is located (State B), while nonbusiness dividends are allocated to the state of commercial domicile (State A). So only the $50,000 of rent goes to State B.

questions.q: Lena is a resident of State R, which taxes residents on all income at a flat 6% and allows a credit for taxes paid to other states limited to the State R tax on the income taxed by the other state. Her income is $150,000 of wages earned in State W and $50,000 of investment income. State W taxed her wages at 5%. What is Lena's net State R tax?
questions.exp: State R tax is 6% x $200,000 = $12,000. The credit is the lesser of State W tax ($7,500) or State R tax on the State W wages (6% x $150,000 = $9,000), so $12,000 - $7,500 = $4,500. The $3,000 trap uses the $9,000 limitation as the credit.

questions.q: Omar works for an employer whose only office is in State E and lives in State F. His salary is $260,000. Of his 260 working days, he worked 156 days at the State E office and 104 days at home in State F for his own convenience. State E applies a 'convenience of the employer' rule. How much of Omar's salary is State E-source income?
questions.exp: Under a convenience-of-the-employer rule, days worked at home for the employee's convenience are treated as days worked at the employer's location, so all $260,000 is State E-source. The $156,000 trap allocates by physical work location.

questions.q: A partnership makes a valid elective pass-through entity tax (PTET) election in its state and pays $50,000 of state income tax at the entity level. Ana owns 40%. How does the PTET payment affect Ana's federal return?
choices: Ana claims a $20,000 itemized deduction for state taxes, subject to the SALT cap
There is no federal effect because the tax is paid on the partners' behalf
Ana's distributive share of the partnership's nonseparately stated income is reduced by $20,000
Ana claims a $20,000 federal tax credit
questions.exp: Under Notice 2020-75, a PTET paid by the entity is deductible by the partnership in computing non-separately stated income, so it reduces Ana's share by 40% x $50,000 = $20,000 and is not subject to the individual SALT cap. Treating it as an itemized deduction is the trap the PTET election avoids.

questions.q: Kira is the 100% shareholder of an S corporation with $1,000,000 of ordinary income. Her property taxes alone already exceed her federal SALT deduction cap. The S corporation makes a PTET election and pays $50,000 of state tax (5%). Kira's marginal federal rate is 35%. Ignoring state credits and the QBI deduction, how much federal income tax does the election save her?
questions.exp: Because her SALT cap is already used, paying the state tax individually yields no federal deduction, while the entity-level payment reduces her flow-through income by $50,000, saving 35% x $50,000 = $17,500. The $50,000 trap treats the payment as a credit rather than a deduction.

questions.q: Hale Corp. bought equipment for $40,000 in State Y and paid State Y sales tax of 4% ($1,600). It immediately moved the equipment to its plant in State X, where the sales/use tax rate is 6%. State X gives credit for sales tax properly paid to another state. How much State X use tax does Hale owe?
questions.exp: State X use tax is 6% x $40,000 = $2,400, less the $1,600 credit for State Y tax paid, so $800 is due. The $2,400 trap ignores the credit; $0 wrongly assumes paying any state's tax ends the obligation.

questions.q: Which of the following activities in State T would cause an out-of-state seller of tangible goods to lose Public Law 86-272 protection from State T net income tax?
choices: Sending catalogs and advertising to State T residents
Having sales reps carry free samples used only for display
Holding a sales meeting for its State T sales reps in a rented hotel room
Owning a warehouse in State T that holds inventory for delivery to customers
questions.exp: Maintaining inventory in the state for filling orders is not solicitation or ancillary to it, so protection is lost. Advertising, occasional sales meetings and display samples are all within the safe harbor.

questions.q: Vance Co. only solicits orders in State T for tangible goods that are approved and shipped from outside the state. State T imposes both a corporate net income tax and a gross receipts tax with economic nexus thresholds, which Vance exceeds. What is Vance's State T exposure?
choices: It owes neither tax
It owes the net income tax but is protected from the gross receipts tax
It is protected from the net income tax but owes the gross receipts tax
It owes both taxes
questions.exp: P.L. 86-272 restricts only taxes imposed on or measured by net income; it does not protect against gross receipts taxes. Assuming the protection covers every state business tax is the trap.

questions.q: CloudCo sells software-as-a-service subscriptions. State Q uses a single sales factor with market-based sourcing for services. CloudCo's receipts from State Q customers are $6,000,000 of $24,000,000 total, and none of its costs of performance occur in State Q. CloudCo has economic nexus in State Q. If apportionable income is $2,000,000, what is State Q apportioned income?
questions.exp: Market-based sourcing assigns receipts to where the customer receives the benefit: $6,000,000 / $24,000,000 = 25% x $2,000,000 = $500,000. The $0 trap applies cost-of-performance sourcing; P.L. 86-272 does not protect services, so nexus exists.

questions.q: Elm Corp.'s State P property factor values owned property at average original cost and rented property at eight times annual rent. In State P, owned property cost $4,000,000 at the beginning of the year and $6,000,000 at the end, and annual rent is $250,000. Everywhere, average owned property is $15,000,000 and annual rent is $500,000. What is Elm's State P property factor (rounded)?
questions.exp: State P: $5,000,000 average owned + 8 x $250,000 = $7,000,000; everywhere: $15,000,000 + 8 x $500,000 = $19,000,000; $7,000,000 / $19,000,000 = 36.8%. The 33.9% trap uses rent at face rather than capitalizing it at eight times.

questions.q: For 2025, assume the federal SALT itemized deduction cap is $40,000, reduced (but not below $10,000) by 30% of modified AGI over $500,000. A married couple filing jointly has MAGI of $560,000 and paid $55,000 of state income and property taxes. What is their SALT deduction?
questions.exp: The cap is reduced by 30% x ($560,000 - $500,000) = $18,000, giving $40,000 - $18,000 = $22,000, which is above the $10,000 floor. The $40,000 trap ignores the income phase-down.

questions.q: Spark Corp. deducted a $3,000,000 royalty paid to its affiliated intangible holding company, which pays no state income tax. Spark's federal taxable income is $5,000,000. State H requires related-party royalties to be added back and apportions 40% of Spark's income to State H. What is Spark's State H taxable income?
questions.exp: The addback raises pre-apportionment income to $5,000,000 + $3,000,000 = $8,000,000, and 40% is $3,200,000. The $2,000,000 trap ignores the addback statute aimed at intangible holding company planning.

questions.q: State N decoupled from federal bonus depreciation. Moss Co.'s federal taxable income of $1,000,000 reflects $600,000 of bonus depreciation on equipment; State N instead allows regular MACRS depreciation of $120,000 on that equipment. What is Moss's State N taxable income before apportionment?
questions.exp: Add back the $600,000 of bonus and subtract the $120,000 State N depreciation: $1,000,000 + $600,000 - $120,000 = $1,480,000. The $1,600,000 trap forgets the state's own depreciation deduction.

questions.q: Ridge Corp.'s federal taxable income is $800,000, after deducting $40,000 of state income taxes. It includes $25,000 of U.S. Treasury interest, and Ridge also earned $15,000 of interest on another state's municipal bonds (excluded federally). State L requires add-back of state income taxes and other states' municipal interest, and subtracts federal obligation interest. What is Ridge's State L taxable income?
questions.exp: $800,000 + $40,000 state tax + $15,000 other-state muni interest - $25,000 Treasury interest = $830,000. States cannot tax federal obligation interest, so adding it back instead of subtracting it (the $880,000 trap) is wrong.

questions.q: Dana, a longtime resident of high-tax State H, expects to sell her closely held stock for a $10 million gain next year and is moving to State Z, which has no income tax. Which planning step best supports sourcing the gain to State Z?
choices: Changing domicile to State Z before the sale by moving her home, family and ties there and severing State H ties
Having the buyer pay the purchase price into a State Z bank account
Keeping her State H home but registering to vote in State Z
Signing the sale contract while temporarily staying in a State Z hotel
questions.exp: Gain from intangibles is generally sourced to the seller's state of residence (domicile) when the gain is realized, so Dana must establish a real change of domicile before the sale. Where the contract is signed or the money is deposited does not decide residency, and keeping the State H home weakens her claim.

questions.q: State G uses post-apportionment NOLs and has no percentage limitation. Birch Corp. had a federal loss of $1,000,000 in Year 1, when its State G apportionment was 40%. In Year 2, Birch had $2,000,000 of income and 25% apportionment. What is Birch's Year 2 State G taxable income?
questions.exp: The Year 1 State G NOL is 40% x $1,000,000 = $400,000; Year 2 apportioned income is 25% x $2,000,000 = $500,000, so $500,000 - $400,000 = $100,000. The $250,000 trap uses the pre-apportionment method ((2,000,000 - 1,000,000) x 25%).

questions.q: Tech Co. has an engineer working full time from her home in State V designing products; Tech's only other State V activity is soliciting sales of its tangible products. What is the most likely State V income tax result?
choices: Tech has nexus only for State V payroll withholding
Tech is protected because the engineer works from a residence, not a business location
Tech has nexus and loses P.L. 86-272 protection because the engineer's work is not solicitation
Tech is protected by P.L. 86-272 because it sells only tangible property
questions.exp: An in-state employee doing non-solicitation work such as engineering establishes physical presence beyond the safe harbor, so P.L. 86-272 protection is lost. Working from home does not change the nature of the activity.

questions.q: State K imposes a 0.26% gross receipts tax on receipts sourced to the state in excess of a $1,000,000 annual exclusion. Atlas Co. has $5,000,000 of State K-sourced receipts and only solicits orders for tangible goods there. What is Atlas's State K gross receipts tax?
choices: $0, because of P.L. 86-272
questions.exp: Tax = 0.26% x ($5,000,000 - $1,000,000) = $10,400. P.L. 86-272 does not apply to gross receipts taxes, and $13,000 ignores the exclusion.

questions.q: In 2024, Kim paid $9,000 of state income tax and $2,500 of property tax, deducting $10,000 under the SALT cap then in effect; her total itemized deductions exceeded her standard deduction by $6,000. In 2025 she received a $3,000 state income tax refund. How much of the refund is included in her 2025 gross income?
questions.exp: Under the tax benefit rule, her correct 2024 taxes were $6,000 + $2,500 = $8,500, so she deducted $10,000 - $8,500 = $1,500 more than she would have; that $1,500 is income. Including the full $3,000 ignores the cap that limited the original benefit.

questions.q: Ivy Partners, a multistate partnership, apportions 30% of its income to State K. Nonresident partner Joel's distributive share of partnership business income is $200,000, and State K taxes nonresidents at 5%. What is Joel's State K tax on this income?
choices: $0, because Joel is a nonresident
questions.exp: Joel's State K-source income is 30% x $200,000 = $60,000, and 5% x $60,000 = $3,000. Nonresidents are taxed on income from in-state sources, so $0 is wrong, and $10,000 taxes his entire share.

questions.q: Parent Corp. owns 100% of three subsidiaries. Which subsidiary is most likely NOT part of Parent's unitary business for combined reporting?
choices: A passively held hotel subsidiary in an unrelated industry with its own independent management and no intercompany transactions
A sales subsidiary that distributes only Parent's products using Parent's centralized purchasing
A manufacturing subsidiary whose output is sold entirely to Parent
A subsidiary sharing Parent's executives, cash management and intercompany financing
questions.exp: Unitary status depends on functional integration, centralized management and economies of scale, not just common ownership. A separately managed, unrelated business with no flow of value is generally not unitary.

questions.q: Glow Inc.'s State J employees earned $1,200,000 of wages and it paid $400,000 to independent contractors working in State J. Everywhere, employee wages were $4,000,000 and contractor fees were $1,000,000. State J's payroll factor includes only compensation paid to employees. What is Glow's State J payroll factor?
questions.exp: Only employee compensation counts: $1,200,000 / $4,000,000 = 30%. Including contractor fees in the numerator and denominator gives the 32% trap.

questions.q: Nova LLC learns it has had sales tax nexus in State W for eight years but never registered or collected tax. Which approach generally limits its exposure most effectively?
choices: Waiting for State W to audit, since the statute of limitations has run on the earlier years
Entering a voluntary disclosure agreement, which typically limits the look-back period and waives penalties, though tax and interest are owed
Registering now and collecting only on future sales, without reporting past periods
Filing amended federal returns to deduct the uncollected tax
questions.exp: A VDA typically limits look-back to about three or four years and waives penalties in exchange for paying tax and interest. When no return was filed, the limitations period generally never starts, so waiting for an audit leaves all eight years open.

questions.q: State Q conforms to the Internal Revenue Code as in effect on a fixed date of January 1, 2024. In 2025, Congress enacts a provision that increases a deduction for businesses. Absent further State Q legislation, how is the new federal provision treated in computing State Q taxable income?
choices: It applies, but only to C corporations
It does not apply; a State Q modification is needed to reverse the federal change
It applies only to taxpayers that elect it
It applies automatically, because State Q starts from federal taxable income
questions.exp: Under static (fixed-date) conformity, later federal changes do not flow through until the state updates its conformity date, so taxpayers must make a modification. Automatic adoption describes rolling conformity, which is the trap.

questions.q: A professional athlete's $3,000,000 salary covers 200 duty days. He spent 10 duty days in State P, which allocates nonresident athletes' compensation by duty days. How much of his salary is State P-source income?
questions.exp: $3,000,000 x 10 / 200 = $150,000. Nonresidents are taxable on compensation for services performed in the state, so $0 is wrong.

questions.q: Merit Corp. wants to minimize state taxes. It does business in State A (single sales factor, separate-entity filing) and wants to move its trademarks into a subsidiary in a no-tax state and pay it royalties. Which state rule most directly defeats this plan?
choices: A throwback rule
A double-weighted sales factor
A fixed-date IRC conformity rule
A related-party expense addback statute or mandatory unitary combined reporting
questions.exp: Addback statutes deny the royalty deduction, and combined reporting eliminates intercompany royalties, so either neutralizes intangible holding company planning. Throwback and factor weighting affect apportionment, not the deduction.

questions.q: In a combined reporting state that has enacted a water's-edge election, what is the main effect of a unitary group making the election?
choices: The group files on a separate-entity basis
The group's apportionment switches to a three-factor formula
Foreign-incorporated affiliates are generally excluded from the combined group, with their income and factors removed
Only affiliates with in-state nexus are included
questions.exp: A water's-edge election generally limits the combined group to domestic (and certain specified foreign) members instead of a worldwide combination. It does not end combined reporting or change the apportionment formula.

questions.q: Seller Co. accepted a properly completed resale certificate in good faith from Buyer, Inc. Buyer later used the goods internally instead of reselling them. Who is liable for the tax on the goods?
choices: Seller and Buyer jointly and severally
Seller Co., because it made the sale
Neither party, because a resale certificate was issued
Buyer, Inc., which owes use tax on the goods it used
questions.exp: A seller that accepts a valid exemption certificate in good faith is generally relieved of liability, and the purchaser that uses the goods owes use tax. The certificate shifts the liability rather than removing the tax.

questions.q: State M uses a factor-presence nexus standard for its corporate income tax: nexus exists if in-state sales exceed $500,000. Quill Advisory, with no in-state property or employees, earned $600,000 of consulting fees from State M clients. What is Quill's State M income tax status?
choices: Taxable, because it exceeds the factor-presence threshold and P.L. 86-272 does not cover services
Not taxable, because physical presence is required for income tax nexus
Taxable only if it has 200 or more State M clients
Not taxable, because P.L. 86-272 protects it
questions.exp: Many states assert economic nexus for income taxes, and P.L. 86-272 protects only solicitation of tangible personal property sales, not services. The 200-transaction test is a sales tax concept.

questions.q: Ward has wages of $180,000: $120,000 from work performed in State C (a nonresident state, tax 4%) and $60,000 from work in his home State D (tax 5% on all income). State D credits taxes paid to other states up to the State D tax on the same income. What is Ward's total state income tax?
questions.exp: State C tax is 4% x $120,000 = $4,800. State D tax is 5% x $180,000 = $9,000, less a credit of $4,800 (lesser of $4,800 or 5% x $120,000 = $6,000), or $4,200. The total is $4,800 + $4,200 = $9,000. The $13,800 trap ignores the credit.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the general rule for sourcing a sale of tangible personal property in the sales factor under UDITPA?
choices: To the state where the sales office that negotiated the sale is located
To the state where the goods were manufactured
To the state where the goods are delivered or shipped to the purchaser
To the state of the seller's commercial domicile
questions.exp: UDITPA sources sales of tangible personal property to the destination state, subject to throwback when the seller is not taxable there. Sourcing by manufacturing location or office is an origin approach the destination rule replaced.

topics.topic: Net operating losses and the §163(j) interest limitation

questions.q: Pax Corp. has 2025 taxable income of $500,000 before any NOL deduction and a $600,000 NOL carryforward from 2021. What is Pax's 2025 NOL deduction, and how much carries forward to 2026?
choices: $500,000 deducted; $100,000 carried forward
$600,000 deducted; $0 carried forward
$480,000 deducted; $120,000 carried forward
$400,000 deducted; $200,000 carried forward
questions.exp: Post-2017 NOLs are limited to 80% of taxable income before the NOL deduction: 80% x $500,000 = $400,000, leaving $200,000 to carry forward indefinitely. Deducting $500,000 ignores the 80% limit.

questions.q: Yule Corp. has 2025 taxable income of $400,000 before NOLs. It has a $100,000 NOL carryforward from 2016 and a $500,000 NOL carryforward from 2020. What is Yule's 2025 taxable income?
questions.exp: The pre-2018 NOL is used first without the 80% limit ($100,000), and the post-2017 NOL is then limited to 80% of the remaining $300,000 = $240,000, so taxable income is $400,000 - $340,000 = $60,000. The $80,000 trap applies the 80% limit to the full $400,000.

questions.q: Under current law, which 2025 net operating loss may be carried back?
choices: A farming loss, which may be carried back two years unless the taxpayer elects to waive the carryback
A loss incurred by a C corporation in its first three years of operation
Any corporate NOL, two years, at the taxpayer's election
No NOLs may be carried back
questions.exp: Most post-2020 NOLs can only be carried forward, but farming losses (and certain insurance company losses) keep a two-year carryback, which can be waived. The CARES Act's five-year carryback applied only to 2018 through 2020 losses.

questions.q: Assume a 2025 standard deduction of $15,000. Ivy, a single sole proprietor, has a $80,000 Schedule C loss, $30,000 of wages and $5,000 of interest income, and claims the standard deduction. What is Ivy's 2025 net operating loss?
questions.exp: Taxable income is $30,000 + $5,000 - $80,000 - $15,000 = -$60,000. Nonbusiness deductions (the standard deduction) are allowed only up to nonbusiness income ($5,000), so $10,000 is added back, giving an NOL of $50,000. The $60,000 trap ignores the §172 modification.

questions.q: Ivo, an individual, has a 2025 NOL. Which deduction is NOT allowed in computing the amount of his NOL?
choices: The §199A qualified business income deduction
Losses from his rental real estate trade or business
Ordinary loss on sale of business equipment
Business expenses of his sole proprietorship
questions.exp: The §199A deduction is not allowed in computing an NOL (§172), and personal exemptions are also disallowed. Business expenses and business losses are exactly what create an NOL.

questions.q: Assume the 2025 excess business loss threshold for a single taxpayer is $313,000. Rhea, single, has a $500,000 net loss from her sole proprietorship (after passive and at-risk limits) and $100,000 of wages. Under §461(l), how much of the business loss is disallowed and carried forward as an NOL?
questions.exp: Wages are not trade or business income for §461(l), so the excess business loss is $500,000 - $313,000 = $187,000, which is carried forward as an NOL. The $87,000 trap wrongly nets the wages against the loss.

questions.q: Elm Corp. has $400,000 of gross income, including a $100,000 dividend from a 20%-owned domestic corporation, and $420,000 of deductible expenses before the dividends-received deduction. What is Elm's NOL for the year?
questions.exp: Taxable income before the DRD is -$20,000. Because the 65% DRD ($65,000) creates or adds to an NOL, the taxable income limit does not apply, and the NOL is $20,000 + $65,000 = $85,000. The $20,000 trap leaves out the DRD.

questions.q: Cobra Corp. has a $50,000 net capital loss and a $200,000 operating loss this year. How are these losses treated?
choices: Both are combined into a $250,000 NOL carried forward indefinitely
The capital loss offsets ordinary income up to $3,000
The $200,000 is an NOL carried forward indefinitely, and the $50,000 net capital loss is carried back 3 years and forward 5 years against capital gains only
The capital loss becomes part of the NOL but is limited to 80%
questions.exp: Corporations cannot deduct net capital losses against ordinary income; they carry them back three years and forward five under §1212, separate from the NOL. The $3,000 allowance is an individual rule.

questions.q: Loss Corp. undergoes a §382 ownership change. Its stock value immediately before the change is $10,000,000, and the applicable long-term tax-exempt rate is 3.4%. Loss Corp. has no built-in gains or losses. What is the annual §382 limitation on its pre-change NOLs?
questions.exp: The §382 limitation is the old loss corporation's value times the long-term tax-exempt rate: $10,000,000 x 3.4% = $340,000 per year. The $800,000 trap applies the 80% NOL limit, which is a different restriction.

questions.q: After an ownership change, the new owners of Loss Corp. discontinue its historic business and do not use a significant portion of its historic assets in a business. This happens within two years of the change. What is the effect on Loss Corp.'s pre-change NOLs?
choices: The §382 limitation becomes zero (except for certain built-in gains and §338 gain), effectively eliminating the NOLs
The §382 limitation is doubled
There is no effect, because continuity of business enterprise matters only for reorganizations
The NOLs become subject to the 80% limit only
questions.exp: §382 sets the limitation to zero if the new loss corporation does not continue the old business enterprise for two years after the change. This continuity requirement is separate from reorganization qualification.

questions.q: Loss Corp. has a net unrealized built-in gain and a §382 base limitation of $340,000. In the first post-change year, it sells an appreciated asset held at the change date, recognizing $200,000 of built-in gain (within its NUBIG). What is the §382 limitation for that year?
questions.exp: Under §382, recognized built-in gain during the five-year recognition period increases the annual limitation: $340,000 + $200,000 = $540,000. Subtracting the gain gives the $140,000 trap.

questions.q: Publico's stock is widely held, with no 5% shareholders. During a two-year period, which set of transactions results in a §382 ownership change?
choices: Investor A buys 30% and investor B buys 25% from the public
Many small public investors trade 80% of the stock among themselves
Investor A buys 45% in one purchase
Investor A buys 30% and investor B buys 15% from the public
questions.exp: An ownership change occurs when 5% shareholders' ownership increases by more than 50 percentage points over a three-year testing period; 30 + 25 = 55 points. Trading among less-than-5% public shareholders does not count, and 45 points falls short.

questions.q: For a tax year beginning in 2025, assume adjusted taxable income (ATI) for §163(j) adds back depreciation, amortization and depletion. Vex Corp. has taxable income of $1,200,000 before business interest expense, after deducting $400,000 of depreciation. It has $600,000 of business interest expense and no interest income. How much business interest expense is disallowed?
questions.exp: ATI = $1,200,000 + $400,000 depreciation = $1,600,000; 30% = $480,000 allowed, so $600,000 - $480,000 = $120,000 is disallowed and carried forward. The $240,000 trap uses EBIT without the depreciation add-back.

questions.q: Wren Corp. is subject to §163(j). It has business interest income of $50,000, ATI of $1,000,000 and business interest expense of $400,000, with no floor plan financing. What amount of business interest expense may Wren deduct?
questions.exp: The limitation is business interest income plus 30% of ATI: $50,000 + $300,000 = $350,000, so $50,000 is carried forward. Leaving out the business interest income gives the $300,000 trap.

questions.q: Assume the 2025 §448 gross receipts threshold is $31 million. Which taxpayer is exempt from the §163(j) business interest limitation in 2025?
choices: A C corporation with $45 million of average gross receipts
A syndicate partnership (a tax shelter) with $2 million of gross receipts
A partnership with $60 million of receipts that elects to capitalize its interest
An S corporation with average gross receipts of $18 million for the prior three years that is not a tax shelter
questions.exp: The small business exemption applies to taxpayers (other than tax shelters) that meet the §448 gross receipts test. Tax shelters, including syndicates, cannot use the exemption whatever their size.

questions.q: Cove Corp. had $120,000 of business interest expense disallowed under §163(j) in 2025. What happens to the disallowed amount?
choices: It is permanently lost
It is carried forward indefinitely and treated as business interest paid in the next tax year, subject to that year's limitation
It is capitalized into the basis of Cove's assets
It is carried forward five years
questions.exp: Disallowed business interest of a C corporation carries forward indefinitely and is treated as paid or accrued in the next year, where it is tested again under §163(j). The carryforward is also a pre-change loss for §382 purposes.

questions.q: Pine Partners has ATI of $1,000,000 and business interest expense of $400,000. Partner Ana has a 50% interest. How is the §163(j) limitation applied?
choices: Pine carries forward $100,000 at the partnership level

The partnership deducts $300,000; $50,000 of excess business interest expense is allocated to Ana, who reduces her basis by $50,000 now and may deduct it only in a future year when Pine allocates her excess taxable income
The partnership deducts $400,000, and Ana applies the limitation on her own return
Ana deducts her $200,000 share subject to her own ATI
questions.exp: For partnerships, §163(j) applies at the entity level; excess business interest expense ($100,000) is allocated to partners, reduces their basis immediately, and is carried forward at the partner level until the same partnership allocates excess taxable income. Partnership-level carryforward is the S corporation rule.

questions.q: Lake Partners has ATI of $1,000,000 and business interest expense of $200,000 (no interest income). Partner Jo owns 50%. How much excess taxable income is allocated to Jo?
questions.exp: Unused capacity is $300,000 - $200,000 = $100,000; ETI = ($100,000 / $300,000) x $1,000,000 = $333,333, and Jo's 50% share is $166,667. Allocating the $100,000 of unused capacity directly (Jo: $50,000) is the trap.

questions.q: A real estate partnership makes the irrevocable election to be an electing real property trade or business under §163(j). What is a consequence of the election?
choices: It must use the alternative depreciation system for nonresidential real property, residential rental property and qualified improvement property, so bonus depreciation is unavailable for that property
Its interest is limited to 30% of ATI
It may revoke the election once its gross receipts exceed the threshold
It must change to the accrual method
questions.exp: The election takes the real property business out of §163(j) entirely, but requires ADS for these property types (for example, 30 years for residential rental and 20 years for QIP, with no bonus). The election is irrevocable.

questions.q: AutoMart, a car dealer subject to §163(j), has ATI of $800,000, floor plan financing interest of $200,000 and other business interest expense of $300,000. How much business interest expense is disallowed?
questions.exp: The limit is 30% x $800,000 + floor plan interest of $200,000 = $440,000. Total interest is $500,000, so $60,000 is disallowed. The $260,000 trap ignores the separate floor plan allowance.

questions.q: For a tax year beginning in 2025, assume ATI is taxable income computed without business interest expense, business interest income, the NOL deduction, and depreciation and amortization. Fox Corp.'s taxable income is $500,000 after a $100,000 NOL deduction, $300,000 of business interest expense, $20,000 of business interest income and $150,000 of depreciation. What is Fox's ATI?
questions.exp: ATI = $500,000 + $100,000 + $300,000 - $20,000 + $150,000 = $1,030,000. Interest income is subtracted because it is counted separately in the limitation; adding it gives the $1,070,000 trap.

questions.q: For a tax year beginning in 2025, Gale Corp. has taxable income of $1,000,000 before business interest expense and NOLs (ATI also $1,000,000), business interest expense of $500,000, and a $1,000,000 post-2017 NOL carryforward. What is Gale's taxable income?
questions.exp: §163(j) is applied first: 30% x $1,000,000 = $300,000 allowed, leaving $700,000. The NOL is then limited to 80% x $700,000 = $560,000, so taxable income is $140,000. Deducting all $500,000 of interest gives the $100,000 trap.

questions.q: Silo, Inc., an S corporation subject to §163(j), has $80,000 of business interest expense disallowed this year. How is the disallowed amount treated?
choices: It is converted into an NOL
It is carried forward at the S corporation level and deducted in a future year subject to the S corporation's limitation
It passes through to shareholders as excess business interest expense, reducing their stock basis
It is permanently disallowed
questions.exp: Unlike partnerships, S corporations carry disallowed business interest forward at the corporate level. The partner-level EBIE regime does not apply to S corporations.

questions.q: Oak Corp. has a 2016 NOL carryforward. Through which tax year may it be carried forward?
choices: Indefinitely
questions.exp: NOLs arising in tax years beginning before 2018 keep the 20-year carryforward period, so a 2016 NOL expires after 2036. Indefinite carryforward applies only to losses from 2018 and later.

questions.q: Ned, single, has 2025 taxable income of $200,000 before his NOL and QBI deductions, and a $250,000 NOL carryforward from 2022. What is his NOL deduction for 2025?
questions.exp: The 80% limit also applies to individuals and is computed without the NOL and §199A deductions: 80% x $200,000 = $160,000, with $90,000 carried forward. Deducting $200,000 ignores the limit.

questions.q: Rhea had a $187,000 excess business loss disallowed in 2025 under §461(l). How is it treated in 2026?
choices: It is again tested under the excess business loss threshold as a current business loss
It is lost
It is treated as part of her NOL carryforward to 2026, subject to the 80% NOL limitation
It is deductible in full in 2026 without limitation
questions.exp: Disallowed excess business losses become NOL carryforwards and are deducted under the NOL rules, including the 80% limit. They are not retested as current-year business losses.

questions.q: Lou is a 50% partner whose outside basis is $200,000, already reduced by $50,000 of excess business interest expense allocated to him and never deducted. He sells his entire interest for $300,000 (no liabilities). What is his gain?
questions.exp: Immediately before disposing of the interest, the partner increases basis by the unused EBIE: $200,000 + $50,000 = $250,000, so the gain is $300,000 - $250,000 = $50,000. The EBIE itself is never deducted.
