questions.q: For a tax year beginning in 2025, assume §163(j) ATI adds back depreciation. Compared with 2022 through 2024, when depreciation was not added back, what is the effect on Mill Corp.'s §163(j) limitation if it claims 100% bonus depreciation on $2,000,000 of equipment in 2025?
choices: Its ATI falls by $2,000,000, reducing its interest deduction by $600,000
Its interest deduction falls by $2,000,000
Its interest deduction is unaffected because the business is exempt
The bonus depreciation does not reduce ATI, so claiming it does not reduce the allowable interest deduction
questions.exp: With the depreciation add-back, ATI is effectively an EBITDA measure, so bonus depreciation reduces taxable income without reducing the interest capacity. Under the 2022-2024 EBIT rule, the bonus would have cut ATI and the limit by 30% x $2,000,000 = $600,000.

questions.q: Hal has $30,000 of investment interest expense and $18,000 of net investment income (he did not elect to include qualified dividends or capital gains). How much investment interest may he deduct this year?
choices: $18,000 deducted and $12,000 carried forward
$0, because investment interest is subject to §163(j)
$9,000, which is 30% of the expense
questions.exp: Investment interest is limited to net investment income, with the excess carried forward indefinitely. §163(j) applies to business interest, not investment interest.

questions.q: Which of the following businesses is excluded from the §163(j) definition of a trade or business, so its interest is not limited?
choices: A large wholesaler that leases equipment
A regulated public electric utility whose rates are set by a public utility commission
A large manufacturing corporation
A partnership that owns a hotel and did not make any election
questions.exp: §163(j) excludes performing services as an employee, electing real property and farming businesses, and certain regulated utilities. A hotel partnership must elect the real property trade or business exception to escape the limit.

questions.q: A consolidated group of C corporations is subject to §163(j). How is the limitation computed?
choices: Separately for each member, with no sharing of capacity
Separately for each member, using the parent's ATI
Only for the parent, with subsidiaries exempt
On a consolidated basis, using the group's consolidated ATI and business interest, with intercompany interest disregarded
questions.exp: The regulations treat the consolidated group as a single taxpayer for §163(j), so intercompany loans neither create business interest income nor create expense. Separate computation is the trap.

questions.q: Assume the 2025 excess business loss threshold for married filing jointly is $626,000. Jay and Kim file jointly. Jay's business has a $900,000 loss, and Kim's business has $100,000 of net income (both after basis, at-risk and passive limits). What is their excess business loss?
questions.exp: Aggregate business losses net against business income: $900,000 - $100,000 = $800,000, and $800,000 - $626,000 = $174,000 is disallowed. The $274,000 trap fails to net Kim's business income.

questions.q: Assume a 2025 standard deduction of $15,000. Max, single, has a $100,000 sole proprietorship loss, $20,000 of wages, $2,000 of interest income and a $3,000 nonbusiness net capital loss deduction, with no capital gains. He claims the standard deduction. What is his NOL?
questions.exp: Taxable income is $20,000 + $2,000 - $3,000 - $100,000 - $15,000 = -$96,000. Add back the nonbusiness capital loss ($3,000, since there are no nonbusiness capital gains) and the nonbusiness deductions above nonbusiness income ($13,000), for an NOL of $80,000. The $96,000 trap skips the §172 modifications.

questions.q: A highly leveraged C corporation expects large §163(j) disallowances for years. Which financing change would most directly reduce the amount disallowed, assuming the tax and business costs are otherwise equal?
choices: Refinancing with longer-term debt at the same rate
Replacing some debt with operating leases or equity financing, because rent and dividends are not business interest
Lending money to a related partnership
Converting to a cash-method taxpayer
questions.exp: §163(j) limits only business interest, so financing through leases (rent is deductible) or equity reduces the interest subject to the cap. The length of the debt does not change the 30% computation.

questions.q: In what order are the loss limitations applied to an individual's share of a loss from an activity?
choices: Basis, at-risk, passive activity, then excess business loss
Excess business loss, passive activity, at-risk, basis
At-risk, basis, excess business loss, passive activity
Passive activity, basis, at-risk, excess business loss
questions.exp: Losses must first clear the basis limit, then §465 at-risk, then §469 passive activity rules, and only then the §461(l) excess business loss limitation. The other orders would let suspended losses be counted twice.

questions.q: Loss Corp.'s §382 limitation is $340,000 per year. In the first post-change year, its taxable income before NOLs is only $200,000, and it uses $200,000 of pre-change NOLs. Ignoring the 80% limit for simplicity, what is the §382 limitation for the second post-change year?
questions.exp: Unused §382 limitation carries forward and is added to the next year's limitation: $340,000 + ($340,000 - $200,000) = $480,000. Treating the unused $140,000 as forfeited is the trap.

questions.q: Bane Corp. has NOL carryforwards of $100,000 from 2019 and $200,000 from 2021. Its 2025 taxable income before NOLs is $250,000. After the 2025 NOL deduction, what carryforward remains?
questions.exp: The 80% limit allows $200,000 (80% x $250,000), applied oldest first: all $100,000 of the 2019 NOL and $100,000 of the 2021 NOL, so $100,000 of the 2021 loss remains. Using the newer loss first is the trap.

questions.q: Which statement about a corporation's net operating loss under §172 is correct?
choices: The 80% limitation is computed on taxable income determined without the NOL deduction itself and without the §199A and §250 deductions
Capital loss carryovers increase the NOL
Charitable contribution carryforwards are part of the NOL
The NOL deduction is computed after the §250 deduction
questions.exp: §172 measures the 80% limit on taxable income computed without regard to the NOL, §199A and §250 deductions. Capital loss and charitable carryovers are tracked separately from NOLs.

topics.topic: Personal financial planning and retirement accounts

questions.q: Ann, single, age 40, is an active participant in her employer's 401(k) plan and has modified AGI of $86,000. Assume the IRA contribution limit is $7,500, and the deduction phase-out range for an active participant filing single is $81,000 to $91,000. What is the maximum deductible traditional IRA contribution she can make?
questions.exp: She is halfway through the $10,000 phase-out range ($5,000 ÷ $10,000), so the deductible limit is reduced by 50%: $7,500 × 50% = $3,750 under §219(g). Answering $0 treats active participation as an absolute bar, but it only triggers the phase-out.

questions.q: Ben, age 45, is an active participant in his employer's retirement plan, and his wife Cara, age 44, has no earned income and no plan coverage. Their joint modified AGI is $200,000, and Ben's wages easily exceed both contributions. Assume the IRA limit is $7,500 per spouse; the joint phase-out range for an active participant is $129,000 to $149,000; and the phase-out range for a spouse who is not an active participant but is married to one is $242,000 to $252,000. What is the total deductible traditional IRA contribution for the couple?
questions.exp: Ben's MAGI exceeds the top of his range, so his deduction is zero; Cara's deduction uses the higher $242,000–$252,000 range under §219(g), so her full $7,500 spousal IRA contribution is deductible. Answering $0 wrongly applies Ben's active-participant range to Cara.

questions.q: Dev, single, has modified AGI of $156,000. Assume the Roth IRA contribution limit is $7,500 and the Roth phase-out range for single filers is $150,000 to $165,000. What is the maximum Roth IRA contribution Dev can make?
questions.exp: Dev is 6/15 (40%) of the way through the phase-out, so his limit is reduced by 40%: $7,500 × 60% = $4,500 under §408A. Answering $3,000 confuses the 40% reduction with the remaining allowable amount.

questions.q: Eva makes a $7,000 nondeductible contribution to a traditional IRA and converts $7,000 to a Roth IRA a week later. On December 31, after the conversion, her only other IRA, a rollover IRA holding pre-tax money, has a balance of $93,000. She has no other IRA basis. How much of the conversion is taxable?
questions.exp: Under the §408 pro rata rule, all traditional IRAs are combined: basis of $7,000 ÷ ($93,000 + $7,000) = 7% of the conversion is nontaxable ($490), so $6,510 is taxable. The 'backdoor Roth' result of $0 holds only if she has no pre-tax IRA balances at year end.

questions.q: Fred, age 52, withdraws $30,000 from his traditional IRA (no basis): $10,000 for his first home purchase (he has never used this exception), $8,000 for his son's qualified college tuition, and $12,000 to pay credit card debt. What additional tax under §72(t) does Fred owe?
questions.exp: IRA distributions for qualified higher education expenses and up to $10,000 of first-time homebuyer costs are exempt from the 10% additional tax, leaving $12,000 × 10% = $1,200. All $30,000 is still subject to regular income tax. Answering $3,000 ignores the IRA-specific exceptions.

questions.q: Gia separated from service at age 56 and wants to draw $40,000 from her former employer's 401(k) plan this year without the 10% additional tax. Which approach accomplishes this?
choices: Roll the entire balance to an IRA, then withdraw $40,000 from the IRA
Roll the balance to an IRA and take the withdrawal after a 60-day holding period
Take the $40,000 from her IRA under the age-55 separation exception
Leave the money in the 401(k) plan and take the $40,000 distribution directly from the plan
questions.exp: The §72(t) exception for separation from service in or after the year the employee turns 55 applies only to distributions from the employer's qualified plan, not to IRAs. Rolling the money to an IRA first forfeits the exception.

questions.q: Hank, age 45, opened a Roth IRA eight years ago. The account holds $30,000 of contributions (no conversions) and $20,000 of earnings. He withdraws $35,000 for a nonqualified purpose. How much of the withdrawal is included in his gross income?
questions.exp: Roth distributions come out of regular contributions first, tax-free, under §408A ordering rules: $30,000 is a return of contributions and the remaining $5,000 is earnings, which are taxable (and subject to the 10% additional tax) because Hank is under 59½. Answering $14,000 prorates earnings as though the pro rata rule for traditional IRAs applied.

questions.q: Iris, age 75, had a traditional IRA balance of $500,000 on December 31 of last year. Her life expectancy factor under the Uniform Lifetime Table for this year is 24.6. What is her required minimum distribution for this year?
questions.exp: The RMD is the prior year-end balance divided by the distribution period: $500,000 ÷ 24.6 = $20,325. Dividing by 25 or using the current year's balance are common errors.

questions.q: Jake failed to take $20,000 of his required minimum distribution this year. He takes the shortfall and files the required return within the correction window allowed under SECURE 2.0. What excise tax applies to the shortfall?
questions.exp: Section 4974 now imposes a 25% excise tax on an RMD shortfall, reduced to 10% when the failure is corrected timely within the correction window: $20,000 × 10% = $2,000. The $10,000 result uses the former 50% rate.

questions.q: Kim died this year at age 68 with a traditional IRA. Under the SECURE Act, which beneficiary may stretch distributions over his or her own life expectancy instead of emptying the account by the end of the tenth year after death?
choices: Kim's 30-year-old niece
Kim's 64-year-old brother, who is not disabled or chronically ill
A see-through trust for Kim's adult grandchildren
Kim's 40-year-old son, who is in good health
questions.exp: An eligible designated beneficiary under §401 includes an individual not more than 10 years younger than the decedent, so the 64-year-old brother qualifies. Adult children, a niece, and trusts for adult grandchildren are non-eligible designated beneficiaries subject to the 10-year rule.

questions.q: Lena, age 61, earns $300,000 and participates in her employer's 401(k) plan. Assume the elective deferral limit is $24,500, the standard catch-up for those age 50 and over is $8,000, and the enhanced catch-up for those ages 60 through 63 is $11,250. What is the maximum elective deferral Lena can make this year?
questions.exp: SECURE 2.0 replaces the standard catch-up with the higher catch-up for participants ages 60–63: $24,500 + $11,250 = $35,750. Adding both catch-ups ($43,750) is not allowed. Because her prior-year wages are high, the catch-up must be made as Roth contributions, but the dollar limit is unchanged.

questions.q: Mo is a self-employed consultant with $100,000 of Schedule C net profit and no employees. His deduction for one-half of self-employment tax is $7,065. What is the maximum deductible contribution to his SEP IRA, assuming the 25% contribution rate is the plan maximum?
questions.exp: For a self-employed person, the 25% rate is applied to compensation net of the contribution itself, which works out to 20% of net earnings after the half-SE-tax deduction: ($100,000 − $7,065) × 20% = $18,587. Applying 25% directly to $92,935 ($23,234) ignores the circular reduction.

questions.q: Nora owns a business with 12 employees and wants to set up a SEP IRA that makes a 15% contribution for herself. Which statement about the plan is correct?
choices: She must contribute the same percentage of compensation for every eligible employee
Contributions vest over a six-year graded schedule
Employees may make their own salary-deferral contributions to the SEP
She may limit contributions to herself and key employees
questions.exp: SEP contributions must be made at a uniform percentage of compensation for all eligible employees and are immediately 100% vested under §408(k). New SEPs do not allow elective salary deferrals, which are a feature of 401(k) and SIMPLE plans.

questions.q: In Year 1, Omar made a $3,000 excess contribution to his traditional IRA and did not withdraw it, or its earnings, by the due date of his Year 1 return. What excise tax does Omar owe for Year 1 on the excess?
questions.exp: Section 4973 imposes a 6% excise tax on an excess contribution for each year it remains in the account at year end: $3,000 × 6% = $180, and the tax recurs each year until corrected. The $300 figure uses the 10% early-distribution rate, which is a different penalty.

questions.q: Pia received a check for her entire IRA balance in March and redeposited it into another IRA within 60 days. In November, she wants to move a second IRA to a new custodian. Which method avoids a problem with the rollover rules?
choices: Any method, because the one-rollover rule applies per account
Have the funds moved directly from one IRA trustee to the other
Receive the funds and redeposit them within 30 days
Receive a distribution check and redeposit it within 60 days
questions.exp: An individual may make only one IRA-to-IRA indirect (60-day) rollover in any 12-month period, counted across all of the individual's IRAs. Direct trustee-to-trustee transfers are not rollovers and are unlimited. The limit is per taxpayer, not per account.

questions.q: Raj, age 45, left his job and requested a $100,000 lump-sum distribution of his 401(k) (all pre-tax). The plan withheld 20% and paid him $80,000, which he deposited in a rollover IRA within 60 days. He did not replace the withheld amount. How much is included in his gross income?
questions.exp: Only the $80,000 actually rolled over is excluded; the $20,000 withheld is a taxable distribution and is also subject to the 10% additional tax because Raj is under 55 at separation. Answering $0 assumes withholding is just a credit. To roll over the full amount, he would have had to deposit $20,000 of other funds.

questions.q: Sue receives a lump-sum distribution from her employer's 401(k) that includes employer stock with a plan cost basis of $50,000 and an FMV of $300,000. She moves the stock to a taxable brokerage account and does not sell it this year. How much ordinary income does she recognize this year on the stock?
questions.exp: Under §402(e)(4), on a lump-sum distribution of employer securities, only the plan's cost basis ($50,000) is taxed currently as ordinary income; the $250,000 net unrealized appreciation is taxed as long-term capital gain when the stock is sold. Taxing the full FMV ignores the NUA rule.

questions.q: Tom's full retirement age is 67, and his monthly Social Security benefit at that age would be $2,000. Delayed retirement credits accrue at 8% per year. If he waits until age 70 to claim, what will his monthly benefit be, ignoring cost-of-living adjustments?
questions.exp: Delayed retirement credits are simple, not compounded: 8% × 3 years = 24%, so $2,000 × 1.24 = $2,480. Compounding the credits gives $2,519, which overstates the benefit.

questions.q: Una paid $20,000 to buy an existing $200,000 life insurance policy on the life of an unrelated business acquaintance and then paid $10,000 of premiums. The insured died and Una collected $200,000. No exception applies. How much of the proceeds is taxable to Una?
questions.exp: Under the §101 transfer-for-value rule, the exclusion is limited to the consideration paid plus later premiums: $200,000 − ($20,000 + $10,000) = $170,000 taxable. Excluding all the proceeds ignores the rule, and subtracting only the purchase price ($180,000) ignores the premiums.

questions.q: Vince paid $60,000 for a single-life annuity that pays $10,000 a year. The expected return under the annuity is $100,000. How much of each $10,000 annual payment is included in his gross income?
questions.exp: Under §72, the exclusion ratio is investment ÷ expected return = $60,000 ÷ $100,000 = 60%, so $6,000 of each payment is excluded and $4,000 is taxable. The $6,000 answer reverses the excluded and taxable portions.

questions.q: Wen withdraws $20,000 from her daughter's §529 plan and uses it for a family vacation. Contributions make up 70% of the account and earnings 30%. What are the federal tax consequences of the withdrawal?
choices: $6,000 included in income and no additional tax
$20,000 included in income and a $2,000 additional tax
$6,000 included in income and a $600 additional tax
$0 included in income because contributions are withdrawn first
questions.exp: A nonqualified §529 distribution is prorated between contributions and earnings: the $6,000 earnings portion is taxable under §72, plus the §529 10% additional tax ($600). The 'contributions first' rule applies to Roth IRAs, not to §529 plans.

questions.q: Xavier's §529 account for his daughter has been open for 16 years. She finished college with $30,000 left over. Assume the lifetime limit on §529-to-Roth IRA rollovers is $35,000, and the Roth IRA annual contribution limit is $7,500. Which statement about rolling the leftover funds to a Roth IRA for the daughter is correct?
choices: The full $30,000 can be rolled over this year, regardless of her compensation
Contributions made to the §529 account in the last five years (and their earnings) are not eligible, and the yearly rollover is limited to the Roth annual limit reduced by her other IRA contributions
The rollover is subject to the Roth income phase-out based on the daughter's MAGI
The rollover is permitted only to a Roth IRA owned by Xavier
questions.exp: SECURE 2.0 permits §529-to-Roth rollovers for the beneficiary if the account has been open at least 15 years, excludes contributions from the past five years, and limits each year's rollover to the Roth annual limit less her other IRA contributions, up to the lifetime cap. The Roth income phase-out is waived for these rollovers, but she still needs compensation at least equal to the rollover amount.

questions.q: Yara, age 67, withdraws $10,000 from her HSA to pay for a cruise. She has no medical expenses this year. What is the tax effect of the withdrawal?
choices: $0 included in income because she is over 65
$10,000 included in income and a $1,000 additional tax
$10,000 included in income with no additional tax
$10,000 included in income and a $2,000 additional tax
questions.exp: Under §223, a nonqualified HSA distribution is included in income, but the 20% additional tax does not apply after age 65, death, or disability; after 65 an HSA works like a traditional IRA for non-medical withdrawals. The 20% additional tax applies only to those under 65.

questions.q: Zeke, age 76, has $400,000 in a designated Roth account in his former employer's 401(k) plan. Under current law, what are his required minimum distribution obligations for this account?
choices: He must roll the account to a Roth IRA by age 73 to avoid RMDs
He must take RMDs, but they are tax-free
He has no lifetime RMDs from the designated Roth account
He must take RMDs because Roth 401(k) accounts follow the same rules as pre-tax 401(k) accounts
questions.exp: SECURE 2.0 eliminated pre-death RMDs from designated Roth accounts in employer plans starting in 2024, matching the Roth IRA rules. A rollover to a Roth IRA is no longer needed to avoid lifetime RMDs.

questions.q: Ava, a 58-year-old physician with very high, stable earnings and two young employees, wants to shelter the largest possible deductible amount for herself over the next seven years before she retires. Which type of plan is generally best suited to this goal?
choices: A SEP IRA
A defined benefit or cash balance plan
A SIMPLE IRA
A profit-sharing plan without a 401(k) feature
questions.exp: A defined benefit or cash balance plan funds a target benefit, so contributions for an older owner with a short time horizon can far exceed the §415 defined contribution limit that caps SEP and profit-sharing plans. A SIMPLE IRA has the lowest limits of the four.

questions.q: Ben receives $30,000 of long-term disability benefits this year under a group policy. His employer paid all of the premiums, and they were not included in Ben's income. How much of the benefits is taxable?
choices: $30,000 less his cumulative premiums
questions.exp: Under §105, benefits from employer-paid disability coverage whose premiums were excluded from the employee's income are fully taxable. Had Ben paid the premiums with after-tax dollars, the benefits would be excluded under §104, which is the planning point.

questions.q: Cleo, age 50, converted $40,000 from a traditional IRA (no basis) to a Roth IRA three years ago and paid tax on the conversion then. She has made no other Roth contributions or conversions. This year she withdraws the $40,000. What are the tax consequences?
choices: No income tax and no additional tax
$40,000 of income and a $4,000 additional tax
$40,000 of income and no additional tax
No income tax, but a $4,000 additional tax
questions.exp: Converted amounts come out after regular contributions and are not taxed again, but under §408A a conversion withdrawn within five years by someone under 59½ is subject to the 10% additional tax: $40,000 × 10% = $4,000. The five-year clock for conversions is separate from the clock for qualified distributions.

questions.q: Dan, age 16, earned $4,000 working at a grocery store this year and has no other income. Assume the IRA contribution limit is $7,500. What is the maximum Roth IRA contribution that can be made for Dan this year?
choices: $0, because he is a minor
questions.exp: IRA contributions are limited to the lesser of the annual limit or the individual's taxable compensation, here $4,000. There is no minimum age, and a parent may fund the contribution as long as Dan has earned income.

questions.q: Ella, age 50, is the sole beneficiary of her late husband's traditional IRA. She needs to withdraw $50,000 over the next three years for living expenses. Which approach avoids the 10% early-withdrawal penalty on those withdrawals?
choices: Keep the account as an inherited IRA and take the withdrawals from it
Roll the IRA into her own IRA and take withdrawals from it
Take a lump-sum distribution and roll the unneeded portion into her own IRA after 90 days
Treat the IRA as her own and take the withdrawals as a hardship distribution
questions.exp: Distributions to a beneficiary because of the owner's death are exempt from the 10% additional tax under §72(t), but once a spouse rolls or elects to treat the IRA as her own, she is the owner and must be 59½ for penalty-free withdrawals. She can still treat the account as her own later, after turning 59½.

questions.q: Fay has a vested 401(k) balance of $80,000 and has never borrowed from the plan. The plan permits loans to the maximum extent allowed under §72(p). What is the maximum loan she can take without it being treated as a distribution?
questions.exp: Under §72(p), a plan loan is limited to the lesser of $50,000 or the greater of 50% of the vested balance or $10,000: 50% × $80,000 = $40,000. The $50,000 statutory cap applies only when half the vested balance exceeds it.

questions.q: Gus, age 75, still works for an unrelated employer, owns no stock in it, and participates in its 401(k) plan, which allows the still-working exception. He also has a traditional IRA from a former job. Assume RMDs generally begin at age 73. Which RMDs must Gus take this year?
choices: RMDs from both the current employer's 401(k) and the IRA
An RMD from the current employer's 401(k) only
An RMD from the IRA only
No RMDs until he retires
questions.exp: The still-working exception in §401 delays RMDs from the current employer's plan for a participant who is not a 5% owner, but it never applies to IRAs. Assuming no RMDs at all extends the exception to accounts it does not cover.

questions.q: Hal, a high-income earner, wants to make a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution and convert it to a Roth IRA. He also has $200,000 of pre-tax money in a rollover IRA, and his current employer's 401(k) plan accepts roll-ins. What should he do to make the conversion essentially tax-free?
choices: Wait 60 days between the contribution and the conversion
Convert in a different calendar year from the contribution
Open a new IRA at a different custodian for the nondeductible contribution
Roll the $200,000 pre-tax IRA into the 401(k) before December 31 of the conversion year
questions.exp: The §408 pro rata rule aggregates all of a person's traditional, SEP, and SIMPLE IRA balances at year end, but not employer plan balances. Moving the pre-tax IRA into the 401(k) by December 31 leaves only basis in the IRA. Using a different custodian does not help because all IRAs are aggregated.

questions.q: Ivy holds high-yield corporate bonds, a broad stock index fund, and an aggressive small-cap growth fund she expects to grow fastest. She has a taxable account, a traditional IRA, and a Roth IRA. Which asset placement is generally the most tax-efficient?
choices: Bonds in the Roth IRA, small-cap growth fund in the taxable account, and index fund in the traditional IRA
Equal portions of each holding in every account
Bonds in the traditional IRA, small-cap growth fund in the Roth IRA, and index fund in the taxable account
Bonds in the taxable account, small-cap growth fund in the traditional IRA, and index fund in the Roth IRA
questions.exp: Interest taxed at ordinary rates belongs in tax-deferred accounts, the highest-growth assets belong in the Roth, where growth is never taxed, and tax-efficient index funds, with qualified dividends, low turnover, and a basis step-up at death, suit taxable accounts. Placing bonds in the taxable account exposes their ordinary interest to annual tax.

questions.q: Jill, age 52, began taking substantially equal periodic payments from her IRA under §72(t) two years ago to avoid the 10% additional tax. This year she wants to take an extra $25,000 withdrawal. What is the consequence?
choices: The extra withdrawal is penalty-free because the payment series already qualifies
There is no consequence if she resumes the original payments next year
Only the extra $25,000 is subject to the 10% additional tax
The modification triggers the 10% additional tax, plus interest, on all prior payments in the series as well
questions.exp: Changing a SEPP series before the later of five years or age 59½ triggers a recapture tax equal to the 10% additional tax that would have applied to all prior distributions, plus interest. Penalizing only the extra withdrawal understates the cost.

questions.q: Kai, in the 22% bracket today, expects to be in the 32% bracket in retirement. He is choosing between deferring $10,000 of pre-tax salary to a traditional 401(k) or paying tax now and contributing the after-tax amount ($7,800) to a Roth 401(k). Either account will quadruple before withdrawal. How much more after-tax money does the Roth produce?
questions.exp: Traditional: $40,000 × (1 − 32%) = $27,200 after tax. Roth: $7,800 × 4 = $31,200 tax-free. The Roth wins by $4,000 because it locks in the lower current rate. Answering $0 assumes equal tax rates, which would make the two choices equivalent.

questions.q: Lou, age 50, has a whole life policy that became a modified endowment contract. The policy has $100,000 of cash value, and his premiums paid total $70,000. He takes a $40,000 policy loan. What are the tax consequences?
choices: $40,000 of income and a $4,000 additional tax
$30,000 of income and a $3,000 additional tax
$0 income, because the loan is less than his basis
$0 income, because policy loans are not distributions
questions.exp: Loans from a MEC are treated as distributions taxed income-first under §72(e): the first $30,000 (cash value over premiums) is taxable, and §72(v) imposes a 10% additional tax before age 59½ ($3,000). The remaining $10,000 is a tax-free recovery of basis. Non-MEC policy loans would not be taxable.

questions.q: Mae's employer provides her with $250,000 of group-term life insurance and pays the full premium. The IRS uniform premium table cost for her age is $0.15 per $1,000 of coverage per month. How much must be included in Mae's gross income for the year?
questions.exp: Section 79 excludes the cost of the first $50,000 of coverage; the remaining $200,000 is taxed at table rates: 200 × $0.15 × 12 = $360. Using the full $250,000 of coverage ($450) ignores the $50,000 exclusion.

questions.q: Ned, age 66 and retired, receives $60,000 of pension income, $15,000 of dividends, and Social Security. His wife, age 64, works part time and earns $20,000. They file jointly. Which statement about IRA contributions this year is correct?
choices: Ned may contribute because pension income is treated as compensation
Neither spouse may contribute because Ned has no compensation
Only the wife may contribute, limited to her own $20,000 of compensation
Both spouses may contribute because the wife's compensation is enough to support contributions for both
questions.exp: Under the §219 spousal IRA rule, on a joint return each spouse may contribute up to the annual limit as long as their combined contributions do not exceed the couple's combined compensation, and the wife's $20,000 covers both. Pensions, dividends, and Social Security are not compensation.

questions.q: Labco uses the regular research credit. Its current-year qualified research expenses (QREs) are $2,000,000. Its fixed-base percentage times average annual gross receipts for the prior four years produces a base amount of $1,200,000. What is Labco's regular research credit?
questions.exp: The base amount is the greater of $1,200,000 or the 50% minimum base ($1,000,000), so the credit is 20% x ($2,000,000 - $1,200,000) = $160,000. The $200,000 trap uses the 50% minimum base even though the computed base is higher.

questions.q: Biotek elects the alternative simplified credit (ASC). Its current-year QREs are $1,000,000, and its QREs for the three prior years were $600,000, $700,000 and $800,000. What is the ASC?
questions.exp: The ASC is 14% of QREs above 50% of the prior three-year average: 50% x $700,000 = $350,000, and 14% x ($1,000,000 - $350,000) = $91,000. The $42,000 trap subtracts the full $700,000 average instead of 50% of it.

questions.q: Newgen began research in the current year and had no QREs in any of the three preceding tax years. Its current-year QREs are $500,000, and it elects the alternative simplified credit. What is its credit?
questions.exp: When a taxpayer has no QREs in any of the three preceding years, the ASC is 6% of current QREs: 6% x $500,000 = $30,000. The $70,000 trap applies the normal 14% rate with a zero base.

questions.q: Tecno's U.S. research activities this year incurred: $800,000 of taxable wages to employees doing qualified research, $100,000 of supplies used in experimentation, $200,000 paid to an unrelated contractor for qualified research, $50,000 of depreciation on lab equipment, and $40,000 of lab utilities and rent. What are Tecno's total QREs?
questions.exp: QREs are wages ($800,000) + supplies ($100,000) + 65% of contract research ($130,000) = $1,030,000; depreciation, rent and utilities are not QREs under §41. The $1,100,000 trap counts 100% of the contract research.

questions.q: Which of the following activities is most likely qualified research for the §41 credit?
choices: Modifying an existing product to meet one customer's specifications using known techniques after commercial production began
Developing a new manufacturing process through a process of experimentation to resolve technical uncertainty about its design
Customer surveys to see which product features buyers prefer
Research performed at the company's lab in Germany
questions.exp: Qualified research must be technological in nature, aim to develop a new or improved business component, and involve a process of experimentation to eliminate uncertainty. Surveys, adaptation after commercial production and foreign research are excluded by statute.

questions.q: Startco, a qualified small business, has a $700,000 research credit this year and no income tax liability. It makes the maximum payroll tax election, which for this year is $500,000. How much of the credit remains available as an income tax credit carryforward?
questions.exp: Up to $500,000 of the credit can be elected against employer payroll taxes, and the remaining $700,000 - $500,000 = $200,000 stays a general business credit that can be carried forward. Nothing is forfeited, so $0 is wrong.

questions.q: Which company is most likely eligible to elect to apply its research credit against employer payroll taxes for its 2025 tax year?
choices: A company with $8 million of 2025 gross receipts that was formed in 2023
A company formed in 2022 with $3.2 million of 2025 gross receipts and no gross receipts before 2022
A company formed in 2015 with $3 million of 2025 gross receipts
A company with no gross receipts that has been profitable from investment income since 2018
questions.exp: A qualified small business must have gross receipts under $5 million for the year and no gross receipts in any year before the five-year period ending with the current year. The 2015 company fails the five-year test, and the $8 million company fails the receipts test.

questions.q: For its 2025 tax year, Corp X has a $100,000 research credit and elects the reduced credit so its §174A research deduction is not reduced. With a 21% corporate rate, what is the amount of the reduced credit?
questions.exp: Under the §280C election, the credit is reduced by the credit times the maximum corporate rate: $100,000 x (1 - 21%) = $79,000. The $65,000 trap confuses this with the 65% contract research rule.

questions.q: Assume that for tax years beginning after 2024, domestic research and experimental expenditures are deductible in full under §174A, while foreign research expenditures are amortized over 15 years beginning at the midpoint of the year paid. In 2025, a calendar-year corporation incurs $900,000 of domestic and $300,000 of foreign research expenditures. What is its 2025 deduction for these costs?
questions.exp: Domestic costs are deducted in full ($900,000), and foreign costs give half a year of 15-year amortization: $300,000 / 15 x 1/2 = $10,000, for a total of $910,000. The $920,000 trap takes a full year of foreign amortization.

questions.q: A large calendar-year corporation has $600,000 of unamortized domestic research expenditures capitalized under §174 in 2022 through 2024. Assume that for its first tax year beginning after 2024 it may elect to deduct the remaining amount either entirely in 2025 or ratably over 2025 and 2026. If it chooses the ratable option, how much does it deduct in 2025?
questions.exp: Ratably over the two-year period means $600,000 / 2 = $300,000 in 2025 and $300,000 in 2026. The $40,000 trap continues the old five-year amortization pattern instead of the accelerated recovery.

questions.q: In 2025, Sunco places in service energy property costing $1,000,000 and claims a 30% investment tax credit. Under §50, by how much must Sunco reduce the property's depreciable basis?
questions.exp: Depreciable basis is reduced by 50% of the energy investment credit: 50% x $300,000 = $150,000, leaving $850,000. Reducing basis by the full $300,000 credit is the trap.

questions.q: Delta claimed a $300,000 energy investment credit on property placed in service on January 1, Year 1. Delta sells the property on July 1, Year 3, which is after two full years but before three full years of service. How much of the credit is recaptured?
questions.exp: The recapture percentage falls by 20 points for each full year of service: disposition in the third year gives 60%, and 60% x $300,000 = $180,000. The $120,000 trap uses 40%, which applies only after three full years.

questions.q: A clean electricity investment credit facility costing $2,000,000 meets the prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements (raising the base rate from 6% to 30%) and also qualifies for the 10-percentage-point energy community bonus. No other bonus applies. What is the credit?
questions.exp: With PWA met, the rate is 30% + 10 points = 40%, and 40% x $2,000,000 = $800,000. The $640,000 trap treats the bonus as 10% of the 30% rate (32%) rather than an additional 10 percentage points.

questions.q: Buyco, a calendar-year C corporation, pays $920,000 in cash to buy $1,000,000 of transferable clean energy credits under §6418 from an unrelated developer and uses them against its 2025 tax. What are Buyco's tax consequences?
choices: It claims a $920,000 credit, limited to the cash paid
It claims the $1,000,000 credit and reports $80,000 of ordinary income
It deducts the $920,000 and claims a $1,000,000 credit
It claims the $1,000,000 credit; the $920,000 is not deductible, and the $80,000 discount is not income
questions.exp: Under §6418, the buyer claims the full credit, cannot deduct the cash paid, and does not recognize income on the discount, while the seller excludes the cash from income. The credit is not limited to the amount paid.

questions.q: A tax-exempt hospital installs solar energy property eligible for a clean energy investment credit. It has no federal income tax liability. How can it benefit from the credit?
choices: It can sell the credit only through a §6418 transfer
It can make an elective payment election under §6417 and receive the credit amount as a refund
It cannot benefit, because exempt organizations owe no income tax
It can claim the credit against its payroll tax withholding
questions.exp: §6417 lets applicable entities such as tax-exempt organizations and governments treat certain clean energy credits as tax payments refundable in cash. Transfer under §6418 is for entities that are not applicable entities, so it is not the exempt hospital's route.

questions.q: A C corporation that is not subject to the corporate AMT has regular tax liability of $210,000 and $200,000 of general business credits for the year. The §38 limitation allows credits up to net income tax minus 25% of net regular tax liability above $25,000. How much of the credit can it use this year?
questions.exp: The limit is $210,000 - 25% x ($210,000 - $25,000) = $210,000 - $46,250 = $163,750, so $36,250 carries over. The $200,000 trap ignores the limitation.

questions.q: A corporation has $36,250 of general business credits it cannot use this year because of the §38 limitation. What are the carryover rules?
choices: Carry back 1 year, then forward 20 years
Carry forward indefinitely, with no carryback
Carry back 2 years, then forward 5 years
Carry back 3 years, then forward 15 years
questions.exp: Under §39, unused general business credits are carried back 1 year and forward 20 years. Indefinite carryforward applies to post-2017 NOLs, not business credits.

questions.q: Maria is a partner in a partnership with average annual gross receipts of $40 million over the prior three years, which passes a research credit through to her. She is subject to the individual AMT. Which statement is correct?
choices: The credit must be applied against payroll tax
The credit cannot offset AMT because research credits never offset AMT
As an eligible small business, the partnership's research credit can offset Maria's AMT
The credit is converted into a deduction for AMT purposes
questions.exp: Under §38, research credits of an eligible small business (average gross receipts of $50 million or less) can offset AMT, and the test is applied at the partnership and partner levels. The payroll offset is for qualified small businesses with under $5 million of receipts and is elective.

questions.q: Engco performs development work for a customer under a fixed-price contract. Engco is paid whether or not the research succeeds, and the customer gets all rights to the results. How do the research costs affect Engco's research credit?
choices: They are QREs for Engco because Engco performs the work
They are not QREs for Engco because the research is funded
65% of the costs are QREs for Engco
They are QREs for Engco only if it also pays the employee wages
questions.exp: Research is funded, and excluded for the performer, when payment does not depend on success or when the performer keeps no substantial rights. Here both conditions apply, so Engco has no QREs, and the 65% rule applies to the customer instead.

questions.q: Retailco develops software solely for internal general and administrative use (an internal accounting system). Beyond the usual four-part test, what additional standard must the software development meet to qualify for the research credit?
choices: It must be developed outside the United States
It must be sold to third parties within one year
The high threshold of innovation test: it must be innovative, involve significant economic risk, and not be commercially available
It must be funded by a government grant
questions.exp: Internal-use software must also satisfy the high threshold of innovation test under the regulations. Software developed for sale or license does not face this extra test.

questions.q: A developer is deciding between a production tax credit (per kWh over 10 years) and an investment tax credit (percentage of basis) for a new renewable facility. Which factor most favors electing the PTC?
choices: High expected electricity production relative to the facility's capital cost
A plan to sell the facility in Year 2
A very high construction cost with low expected output
A need for the largest possible credit in the year placed in service
questions.exp: The PTC rewards output, so efficient, high-production facilities generally do better with it, while the ITC favors costly projects with modest output and gives an upfront benefit. Selling early also creates ITC recapture risk, which does not support the PTC choice.

questions.q: Assume a production tax credit rate of 3.0 cents per kWh for a facility that meets the prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements. In 2025 the facility produced 50,000,000 kWh, sold 45,000,000 kWh to unrelated utilities, and used 5,000,000 kWh on site. What is the PTC?
questions.exp: The PTC applies only to electricity produced and sold to an unrelated person: 45,000,000 x $0.03 = $1,350,000. The $1,500,000 trap includes the electricity used on site.

questions.q: In 2025, when the §25D residential clean energy credit was 30% of qualified costs, the Lees installed solar panels for $24,000 and battery storage for $6,000 at their home. Their 2025 tax liability before credits is $5,000, and they have no other credits. What is their 2025 credit and the amount carried forward?
choices: $7,200 used; $0 carried forward
$5,000 used; $4,000 carried forward
$5,000 used; $0 carried forward
$9,000 used; $0 carried forward
questions.exp: The credit is 30% x ($24,000 + $6,000) = $9,000. It is nonrefundable, so $5,000 offsets the 2025 tax and the unused $4,000 carries forward under §25D. Batteries of at least 3 kWh capacity qualify.

questions.q: For 2025, assume the §25C energy efficient home improvement credit is 30% of costs, with a $2,000 annual limit for heat pumps, a separate $1,200 aggregate annual limit for other items, and a $600 limit for windows. The Parks spent $10,000 on a qualifying heat pump, $2,000 on qualifying windows and $1,000 on insulation. What is their credit?
questions.exp: Heat pump: 30% x $10,000 = $3,000, limited to $2,000. Windows: $600 (30% x $2,000 = $600). Insulation: $300. The non-heat-pump items total $900, under $1,200, so the credit is $2,000 + $900 = $2,900. The $3,900 trap ignores the heat pump cap.

questions.q: In 2025, Grill Co. hired three Work Opportunity Tax Credit-certified employees. Assume the credit is 40% of first-year wages up to $6,000 for employees who work at least 400 hours, and 25% for those who work 120 to 399 hours. Ann worked 500 hours and earned $9,000; Bo worked 300 hours and earned $5,000; Cy worked 100 hours and earned $1,500. What is the WOTC?
questions.exp: Ann: 40% x $6,000 = $2,400; Bo: 25% x $5,000 = $1,250; Cy: nothing (under 120 hours). The total is $3,650. The $4,400 trap gives Bo the 40% rate.

questions.q: Grill Co. paid $120,000 of wages to WOTC-certified employees and claims a $3,650 Work Opportunity Tax Credit. What is the effect on its wage deduction?
choices: The wages must be capitalized
The wage deduction is reduced by $3,650 to $116,350
No effect, because credits and deductions are independent
The wage deduction is reduced by 21% of the credit
questions.exp: §280C requires the wage deduction to be reduced by the amount of the WOTC, to prevent a double benefit. The 21% reduction is how the reduced research credit election works, not this rule.

questions.q: A startup in its third tax year (so its fixed-base percentage is 3%) has $800,000 of QREs and average annual gross receipts of $10,000,000 for the computation period. What is its regular research credit?
questions.exp: The computed base is 3% x $10,000,000 = $300,000, but the base cannot be less than 50% of current QREs ($400,000), so the credit is 20% x ($800,000 - $400,000) = $80,000. The $100,000 trap uses the $300,000 computed base.

questions.q: Which of the following costs incurred in a qualified U.S. research project is a qualified research expense?
choices: Wages paid to researchers working in the company's Canadian lab
The cost of land purchased for a new research campus
Supplies consumed in building and testing prototypes
Depreciation on lab equipment
questions.exp: Supply QREs include tangible property used and consumed in qualified research, other than land and depreciable property. Foreign research is excluded, so Canadian wages are not QREs.

questions.q: For its 2025 tax year, assume §280C requires the §174A deduction for domestic research expenditures to be reduced by the research credit unless the taxpayer elects a reduced credit. A corporation has $1,000,000 of domestic research expenditures and a $100,000 research credit and does not make the election. What is its §174A deduction?
questions.exp: Without the election, the deduction is reduced by the full credit: $1,000,000 - $100,000 = $900,000. Electing the reduced credit instead gives a $79,000 credit with the full $1,000,000 deduction.

questions.q: A corporation's QREs have grown quickly, but it lacks reliable gross receipts records for the 1984 through 1988 base period, and its gross receipts have grown sharply since then. Which planning recommendation is most appropriate?
choices: Use the payroll tax election to avoid computing a base
Use the regular credit, because it always gives the larger credit
Elect the alternative simplified credit, which depends only on the prior three years' QREs and not on gross receipts
Claim no credit, because base-period records are required for every method
questions.exp: The ASC avoids the fixed-base percentage and gross receipts history altogether, and often beats the regular credit for companies with growing receipts. The payroll election is limited to qualified small businesses and does not remove the need to compute a credit.

questions.q: Parent and its two wholly owned subsidiaries form a controlled group. Only Sub 2 conducts research. How is the group's research credit determined?
choices: Only Sub 2 computes a credit, using its own gross receipts
The group is treated as a single taxpayer for computing the credit, and the credit is allocated among the members
Parent claims the entire credit as the common parent
Each member computes its own credit separately, with no aggregation
questions.exp: Under §41 and its regulations, all members of a controlled group are treated as a single taxpayer to compute the credit, which is then allocated among them based on their stand-alone QREs. This stops companies from manipulating the base by moving research among entities.

questions.q: A taxpayer is preparing an amended return to claim a research credit refund. Under current IRS requirements, which information must the claim include?
choices: Only the total QRE amount and the computed credit
Copies of all payroll records for the year
A signed statement from an engineer certifying the research
The business components, the research activities for each, the individuals who performed them, and the information each sought to discover
questions.exp: The IRS requires refund claims for the research credit to identify each business component, the research activities, the individuals involved and the information sought, along with the QRE totals. Totals alone make the claim deficient.

questions.q: A corporation has research credits in three categories: a carryforward from 2020, a carryforward from 2022, and a current 2025 credit. Its §38 limitation allows only part of them to be used this year. In what order are they used?
choices: 2020 carryforward, then 2022 carryforward, then the 2025 credit
Pro rata among all three
The 2025 credit first, then carryforwards from newest to oldest
The taxpayer may choose any order
questions.exp: General business credits are applied first-in, first-out under §38: carryforwards (oldest first), then current-year credits, then carrybacks. This ordering reduces the risk that old credits expire.

questions.q: Jill, single, has AGI of $150,000 and owns an interest in a low-income housing project that generates a passive low-income housing credit. Her taxable income stays in the 24% bracket even after a $25,000 reduction, and she has no passive income. Under §469, credits are allowed up to the tax on a $25,000 deduction equivalent, phasing out for AGI above $200,000. What is the most credit she can use this year?
choices: $0, because she has no passive income
questions.exp: The deduction equivalent of $25,000 at her 24% marginal rate supports $6,000 of credits, and her AGI is below the phase-out. The low-income housing credit does not require active participation, and $25,000 is a deduction equivalent, not a credit amount.

questions.q: Solarco sells clean energy investment credits to Buyco under §6418. Two years later, Solarco's facility has a recapture event. Who is generally liable for the recapture tax?
choices: Buyco, the transferee, though Solarco must notify Buyco of the event
Solarco, the original owner
Solarco and Buyco equally
Neither, because transferred credits cannot be recaptured
questions.exp: Under §6418 and its regulations, ITC recapture falls on the transferee taxpayer, and the transferor must notify it of the recapture event. Buyers manage this risk through indemnities and insurance in the purchase agreement.

questions.q: A domestic manufacturing company has a $250,000 research credit and $90,000 of regular tax after other credits. Its tentative minimum tax is zero, and it is not a qualified small business. With a 21% rate, which planning action best recovers value from the research credit this year?
choices: Making a payroll tax election
Switching from the ASC to the regular credit
Accelerating taxable income (for example, by forgoing bonus depreciation or other elections) so the credit offsets more tax, if the time value of the credit justifies it
Making an elective payment election under §6417
questions.exp: Because the §38 limitation and low tax liability keep the credit from being used, raising taxable income lets more of the credit be used now. The payroll election requires qualified small business status, and the research credit is not an elective payment credit for a for-profit company.

questions.q: Assume a research credit employee is treated as performing qualified services for 100% of their wages if at least 80% of their time is spent on qualified services (the 'substantially all' rule), and otherwise in proportion to their time. Engineer Kai earned $150,000 and spent 85% of his time on qualified research; technician Lu earned $100,000 and spent 50% of her time on qualified research. What are the wage QREs?
questions.exp: Kai meets the 80% substantially all threshold, so all $150,000 counts; Lu counts 50% x $100,000 = $50,000; the total is $200,000. The $177,500 trap prorates Kai's wages at 85%.

questions.q: Startco, a qualified small business, elects to apply $400,000 of its research credit against payroll taxes. Assume the election offsets employer Social Security tax up to $250,000 first, then employer Medicare tax up to $250,000, and that Startco's employer Social Security tax for the relevant periods is $300,000 with enough Medicare tax to absorb any remainder. How much of the credit offsets employer Medicare tax?
questions.exp: The Social Security portion is capped at $250,000 even though $300,000 of tax is available, so the remaining $400,000 - $250,000 = $150,000 offsets Medicare tax. The $0 trap ignores the $250,000 Social Security cap.
